findings.title: Missing merge metadata is never retried when polling is off
findings.detail: Once the queue marks a run merged, reconciliation only reads a saved poller snapshot and skips the GitHub client. If the queue's one metadata request fails, times out, or is interrupted by a restart, an installation with polling disabled has no later observation to fill the fields. The parent feed can therefore retain the null values this change is meant to fix.
findings.suggestion: Keep incomplete merge metadata eligible for a bounded, retryable GitHub observation, including after restart and when polling is disabled.
findings.failure_scenario: The merge succeeds, the metadata lookup times out, and the daemon restarts with GitHub polling disabled. Subsequent reconciliation passes leave mergedBy and mergedAt null indefinitely.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:624–626 records `this.landed(entry, run, sha, null)` before metadata lookup and returns when no observation arrives. src/integrations/github-notifier.ts:159–168 handles already-merged runs using only `savedSnapshot(store.githubPrData(run.prUrl))`, then unconditionally `continue`s; its comment explicitly says missing metadata must never trigger another fetch. src/integrations/index.ts:50–57 starts no poller when `githubPoll` is false. src/land/queue.ts:145 resumes only `listLandEntries({ active: true })`, excluding the completed landing.
verification.trigger: With GitHub polling disabled and no saved MERGED snapshot, a successful merge is persisted as landed with null metadata, then its metadata lookup times out. After restart, reconciliation skips fetching metadata for the merged runs and the queue does not resume the landed entry, leaving mergedBy and mergedAt null indefinitely.

findings.title: Successful lands no longer mark failed or cancelled runs as merged
findings.detail: The previous land path set merged on the run regardless of its status. The replacement calls resolveMergedRun, which only transitions succeeded, resolved, or needs_human runs. Land requests do not restrict the target run to those statuses, so a PR from a failed or cancelled run can land while its run remains unmerged and has no run.merged event.
findings.suggestion: Preserve the previous merged transition for other eligible run statuses while retaining their existing terminal state.
findings.failure_scenario: A failed run has a delivered PR and an approval; a land request succeeds, but resolveMergedRun returns false because the run status is failed.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:379-381 finishes the entry as `"landed"` and calls `this.store.resolveMergedRun(...)`. src/db/store.ts:1843 handles only `current.status === "resolved" || current.status === "succeeded"`; the remaining path specifies `from: ["needs_human"]` (1851). src/db/store.ts:1808 returns null when the current status is outside `from`. Previously, landed unconditionally called `updateRun(run.id, { merged: true })`.
verification.trigger: A failed or cancelled, unmerged run has a delivered PR and valid approval. Landing succeeds, but resolveMergedRun refuses its status, leaving merged false while the queue reports landed.

findings.title: Consumer-bearing reviews fail against an older daemon
findings.detail: The HTTP-backed MCP server forwards the new consumer property to the daemon. The previous daemon's strict ReviewVerdictSchema rejects that unknown property, so a newer CLI cannot submit an approval with consumer provenance to an older running daemon.
findings.suggestion: Encode the MCP identity in the existing reviewer field before forwarding, while respecting its validation limits, or otherwise provide a compatible payload for older daemons.
findings.failure_scenario: A newer MCP proxy calls limitless_review with consumer set while connected to a daemon from the base release; the daemon rejects the request as an unrecognized key.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/mcp.ts:343-346 forwards `{ ...ReviewVerdictSchema.parse(input), reviewer: "mcp" }`, retaining consumer; :279 sends that input to `/review`, and :225 serializes it unchanged. At base 21f8de5, src/pipeline/review-round.ts:25-32 accepts only verdict, reviewedSha, findings and reviewer, then calls `.strict()`; :154-156 throws `ReviewRefused(..., 400)` on validation failure. src/server/http.ts:532-535 returns that refusal's HTTP status.
verification.trigger: A newer MCP proxy submits limitless_review with consumer set to a base-release daemon. The daemon rejects the unknown consumer key with HTTP 400, preventing the review or approval.

findings.title: A failed metadata lookup can permanently leave merge fields empty
findings.detail: The queue records the land before a single best-effort metadata lookup, then silently discards lookup errors, timeouts, and incomplete observations. Reconciliation skips already-merged runs unless a saved merged snapshot happens to exist, so installations without polling, or without a later usable snapshot, never recover the merger and timestamp.
findings.suggestion: Keep missing merge metadata eligible for bounded later reconciliation, while preserving the completed merge and avoiding another merge operation.
findings.failure_scenario: The PR merge succeeds, but the subsequent GitHub metadata request times out while polling is disabled. The queue reports the entry as landed, and both the parent and round run retain null mergedBy and mergedAt indefinitely.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:624-626 calls `this.landed(entry, run, sha, null)` before awaiting metadata and returns if no matching MERGED observation arrives. The lookup converts errors to null at 645. src/integrations/github-notifier.ts:159-168 handles already-merged runs only through `savedSnapshot(store.githubPrData(run.prUrl))`, then continues without fetching. test/land-queue.test.ts:426-478 explicitly expects null merge metadata after lookup failure or timeout.
verification.trigger: The merge succeeds, its metadata lookup times out, polling is disabled, and no saved MERGED snapshot exists. The entry remains landed with no pending recovery, leaving parent and round merge fields null indefinitely.

findings.title: The reported unpinned request cannot identify a changed head
findings.detail: A request with a nonzero file index and no SHA pins fails schema validation before the saved and recorded PR heads are compared. The resulting message asks for pagination pins even when the head has moved, so it does not give the requested new head for the original failure scenario. The MCP tool's schema validation can reject the request before getChange is called as well.
findings.suggestion: Allow the head state to be diagnosed before returning the missing-pins error, while retaining the pin requirement for actual further reads.
findings.failure_scenario: After a conflict round advances the recorded PR head, limitless_get_change called with {"run":"…","file":1} reports that pins are required instead of reporting the new head.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/mcp-change.ts:28-30 requires `((!q.filesOffset && !q.file && !q.diffOffset && !q.reportOffset) || (q.headSha && q.baseSha))`. Thus file:1 without pins fails validation before head inspection. src/integrations/mcp.ts:528-529 maps that failure to `"Further reads require headSha and baseSha from the first page."`.
verification.trigger: After a conflict round advances the head, {run:"…",file:1} fails schema validation and returns the pins-required error without reporting the new head, leaving the explicitly reported scenario unresolved.

findings.title: The original change-view failure is asserted as a pagination error
findings.detail: The new test sends the same unpinned file request described in the issue but expects the missing-pins response. Its superseded-head cases supply SHA pins, so neither backend test checks that the original request after a conflict head move identifies the changed head and names its replacement. This test therefore passes while the reported defect remains.
findings.suggestion: Add a direct and proxy test that advances the recorded head, calls with only run and file, and asserts a superseded-head reason containing the new SHA.
findings.failure_scenario: The recorded head advances after a conflict round and an agent requests file 1 without pins; the test suite accepts a pagination error that omits the new head.

verification.evidence: test/mcp-proxy.test.ts:128–129 sets `args = { run: c.run.id, file: 1 }` and expects `"Further reads require headSha and baseSha from the first page."`; lines 153–155 assert that error. src/integrations/mcp-change.ts:28–30 requires pins for a nonzero file index, and lines 383–390 return the pagination error before reading the recorded head at line 405. src/integrations/mcp.ts:527–529 likewise maps this validation failure to the pagination message.
verification.trigger: After a conflict round advances the recorded head, call limitless_get_change with {run, file: 1} without pins. Validation returns the pagination error before inspecting the head, omitting the new head requested by item 3; the added test explicitly accepts that outcome.

findings.detail: The new consumer field is passed directly into the reviewer value. recordApproval persists that value, and its database trigger copies it into the review.approved feed summary and data without credential redaction. findings.failure_scenario: An MCP client submits an approval with a consumer name containing a registered API token. The token is stored verbatim in review_approvals and in the review.approved feed item.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/review-round.ts:196-201 derives reviewer with `mcpRequestedBy(parsed.data.consumer)` and passes it directly to `store.recordApproval(...)`. src/feed.ts:36 only prefixes it: `mcpRequestedBy = (consumer: string): string => `mcp:${consumer}``. src/db/store.ts:1518-1522 inserts `reviewer` unchanged via `.run(runId, prUrl, sha, reviewer, Date.now())`. src/db/migrations/20261004T1757-review-rounds.sql:57-58 copies `NEW.reviewer` into both the feed summary and JSON data.
verification.trigger: An otherwise valid MCP approval supplies a consumer name containing a registered API token within the 200-character limit. No redaction occurs before insertion, so the credential persists verbatim in review_approvals and the review.approved feed item.

findings.title: Merge metadata is lost if the post-merge lookup fails or is interrupted
findings.detail: The request says to “fill them from the merge the queue recorded.” The queue marks the entry landed before its only metadata lookup. If that lookup fails, times out, or the daemon restarts between these operations, reconciliation only reads an already saved snapshot and never fetches missing metadata for a merged run. With polling disabled, both runs can retain null fields indefinitely.
findings.suggestion: Make missing merge metadata recoverable after landing and restart, including when polling is disabled.
findings.failure_scenario: A merge succeeds, then the metadata request fails transiently or the daemon stops before it completes; the parent and round remain merged with null mergedBy and mergedAt.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:624-625 persists landing before `await this.mergeMetadata(...)`. Lookup failure or abort returns null (633-646), and 626 exits without enrichment. Startup resumes only `listLandEntries({ active: true })` (145), excluding completed lands. Reconciliation of already-merged runs reads only saved snapshots and skips fetching (src/integrations/github-notifier.ts:159-168).
verification.trigger: After landing is persisted, the metadata request fails or shutdown interrupts it before a MERGED snapshot is saved. Without a later external observation, neither restart nor reconciliation recovers the metadata. This overlaps C4’s underlying defect.

findings.title: Feed consumers can receive and acknowledge the incomplete merge event
findings.detail: The request asks for consistent merge fields in the parent run's `run.merged` feed item. Landing publishes that item with null metadata before the asynchronous lookup; later enrichment edits the existing feed row without issuing a new feed item. A consumer that reads and acknowledges the original event before enrichment never receives the corrected fields.
findings.suggestion: Ensure the published merge event contains the available metadata, or publish a durable update that consumers can observe after enrichment.
findings.failure_scenario: A long-polling consumer receives and acknowledges run.merged immediately after landing while the metadata request is in flight; the later database update is behind its acknowledged cursor.

verification.evidence: src/land/queue.ts:624-625 records the merge with null metadata before an asynchronous lookup. src/db/store.ts:1870-1873 enriches it using `UPDATE feed ... WHERE kind = 'run.merged' AND run_id = ?`, preserving its ID. Feed reads select `WHERE id > ?` (716), and acknowledgment stores `acked_id = max(acked_id, excluded.acked_id)` (765-767).
verification.trigger: A feed consumer reads and acknowledges the initial run.merged item while the metadata lookup is pending. Successful enrichment changes the existing item behind its cursor, so subsequent reads never deliver the corrected merge fields.

findings.title: Explicit file index zero is accepted for an empty change
findings.detail: The request says to name “an unknown file index.” When the change contains no files, index 0 is unknown, but this condition deliberately accepts it and returns an available change view. Because the schema defaults an omitted file to zero, the implementation also loses whether the caller explicitly requested that index.
findings.suggestion: Preserve whether file was supplied and report an unknown index when an explicit index does not exist.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller requests file 0 for a PR whose comparison contains zero changed files; the response is available instead of reporting the unknown index.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/mcp-change.ts:481-483: `const selected = files[q.file]; if (!selected && (q.file > 0 || files.length > 0)) return { available: false, reason: ... };`. verification.trigger: With valid saved heads and locally available comparison commits producing zero changed files, explicitly requesting file:0 returns an available response with an empty diff instead of an unknown-index error.

findings.title: Diffs quoted in reports still expose multiline credentials
findings.detail: The new line-prefix-aware filter is applied only to the diff field. Reports returned by the same tool still pass through literal privacy matching, so a report containing a unified diff with each credential line prefixed by '+' or '-' exposes the credential. The request explicitly includes other outputs that render diffs or requires them to be listed as follow-ups.
findings.suggestion: Apply equivalent line-prefix-aware credential filtering to diff quotations in reports, or explicitly document this output as a follow-up as requested.

A bounded probe confirmed zero matches for the quoted two-line credential.

findings.title: Repeated credential matches make patch filtering quadratic
findings.detail: Every occurrence scans every line range synchronously before paging. findings.title: Keep reviewer execution time out of failed-trial preparation timing
findings.detail: The catch path recomputes preparationMs whenever roundsUsed is absent. Review trials never set roundsUsed, so an exception after the reviewer starts overwrites the already-recorded preparation duration with elapsed time including the reviewer invocation. The reported preparation and trial times are no longer separate for that failure.
findings.suggestion: Record the preparation duration once, and only calculate it in the catch path if preparation did not finish.
findings.failure_scenario: A review invocation runs for several minutes and then throws, for example on an origin-exclusion failure. Its preparationMs includes those minutes even though setup had already completed.

verification.evidence: src/evals/runner.ts:689–690 records completed preparation: `const preparationMs = Date.now() - preparationStarted;` and `trial.details.preparationMs = preparationMs`. The catch at src/evals/runner.ts:1201–1202 overwrites it with `!trial.details.roundsUsed ? { preparationMs: Date.now() - preparationStarted } : {}`. `roundsUsed` is assigned only for implement cases (src/evals/runner.ts:1101–1104). An origin failure escapes after reviewer execution via `if (originFailure) throw originFailure` (src/evals/runner.ts:1073).
verification.trigger: A review finishes setup, spends minutes executing, then reaches the outer catch—for example through an origin-exclusion error. Its preparationMs is overwritten to include reviewer execution time, violating the explicit timing separation requirement.

findings.title: Preserve unrelated patch lines when a credential matches
findings.detail: A match in either complete file causes the entire patch to be replaced with a single placeholder. The request requires mapping matches back to their patch lines and keeping the rest of the file visible. The new tests instead assert the whole-file placeholder, so they encode the behavior that violates the acceptance criterion.
findings.suggestion: Map each match to its contributing old-side and new-side patch lines, withhold those lines before paging, and test that unrelated lines remain visible.
findings.failure_scenario: An added file contains a public first line, a two-line registered credential, and a public final line. The response contains only `[withheld: private text; 1 file]`, so neither public line can be reviewed.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/mcp-change.ts:521–523 returns true when a file layer includes a multiline credential. Lines 539–540 then replace the entire patch: `? (await privateFile(selected.path)) ? "[withheld: private text; 1 file]"`.
verification.trigger: An added file contains public lines surrounding a registered two-line credential. The entire patch is withheld, hiding both public lines and violating the explicit visible-context requirement.

findings.title: Protect or document the other diff-rendering paths
findings.detail: The new inspection applies only to `limitless_get_change`. findings.suggestion: Apply a shared line-prefixed diff redactor to those paths, or explicitly record the affected diff renderers as follow-ups as permitted by the request.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:1394 defines `reviewText` as `redactPrivate(redactGateOutput(text), privateStrings())`; line 1413 applies it to the first-parent diff. src/gates/output.ts:22–23 calls `redactCredentials(stripVTControlCharacters(output))`, whose implementation at src/util/proc.ts:683–684 uses literal `text.split(secret).join("[redacted]")`. src/pipeline/prompts.ts:468 includes `sealedFence(input.firstParentPatch.slice(0, PATCH_LIMIT) || "(empty diff)")`. The change modifies only mcp-change.ts and its tests, with no follow-up documentation.
verification.trigger: A conflict-resolution first-parent patch contains `+alpha-secret\n+beta-secret` for registered credential `alpha-secret\nbeta-secret`. The prefixes prevent literal matching, so both credential halves enter the review prompt.

Verifier: 10 candidates, 10 checked, 1 refuted.

findings.title: A passing retry clears a security check failure
findings.detail: The retry classification treats every check alike: a successful full retry becomes non-blocking flaky, with no way to preserve a security check's failure. The request explicitly requires security failures never to become passes. A direct call to retryRegressions with a failing security-scan followed by a passing retry returned verdict "flaky" and blocking false.
findings.suggestion: Represent which checks are security checks and keep their initial failures blocking regardless of retry outcome.
findings.failure_scenario: A security scan reports a vulnerability on the first post-change run but exits successfully on its retry; the gate becomes non-blocking and the change can proceed.

verification.evidence: src/gates/run.ts:374-383 selects regressed checks without excluding security scans. src/gates/run.ts:393-394 then assigns `verdict: confinementError ? "confinement_error" : retry.ok ? "flaky" : "regressed"` and `blocking: confinementError || !retry.ok`. Only confinement failures receive special protection.
verification.trigger: A security scan passes on baseline, fails after the change without naming a changed location, then passes its full retry. Its failure becomes nonblocking, violating the explicit security-check requirement.

findings.title: Bun's report can omit failed files entirely
findings.detail: Bun's JUnit reporter omits files that fail during module loading when another file has a normal test failure. The parser accepts the remaining report as a complete failure list, so the targeted retry runs even though not all failing files are known. A local Bun reproduction with one failed assertion and a second file throwing at module load produced a report containing only the assertion failure, and parseJUnit returned only that file.
findings.suggestion: Detect incomplete Bun reports, including runner-level or module-load errors, and fall back to the full retry when the complete failure list cannot be established.
findings.failure_scenario: A suite has a failing test in a.test.ts and an import-time exception in b.test.ts. Only a.test.ts is retried; if it fails, the full check is skipped despite b.test.ts being an unknown failing file.

verification.evidence: src/gates/junit.ts:85–88: "else for (const suite of elements(root).filter((child) => child.name === \"testsuite\")) visit(suite);" followed by "if (!validRetryFiles(failedFiles, cwd)) return undefined;" validates listed paths without detecting omitted failures. Reproduced with Bun 1.4.3: an assertion failure in a.test.ts plus an import-time exception in b.test.ts produces JUnit containing only a.test.ts, which parseJUnit accepts. src/gates/run.ts:259–261: "if (confinementFailed(attempt) || (!attempt.ok && !attempt.timedOut))" records the targeted failure and executes "continue;", skipping the full retry.
verification.trigger: An assertion failure and an import-time exception occur in different files. Bun omits the import-error file from JUnit; only the assertion file is retried, and its repeated failure skips the required full fallback for unknown failing files.

findings.title: An incomplete failure list is accepted as complete
findings.detail: A suite reporting multiple failures is accepted when only one failure has a file-bearing testcase. The parser does not reconcile the suite's failure and error counts with the represented failures, so it can choose a targeted retry when the remaining failing files are unknown. The command `bun -e 'import {parseJUnit} from "./src/gates/junit.ts"; console.log(JSON.stringify(parseJUnit(`<testsuite failures="2"><testcase file="test/gate-retry-files.test.ts"><failure/></testcase></testsuite>`, process.cwd())))'` returned `{"failedFiles":["test/gate-retry-files.test.ts"],"failedFileTimes":{}}`.
findings.suggestion: Reject reports whose declared failures cannot all be attributed to files, and fall back to the full retry.
findings.failure_scenario: A report declares two failures but identifies only one failing testcase; the known file is retried alone instead of falling back to the full check.

verification.evidence: src/gates/junit.ts:75 sets "caseFailed = true;" for any identifiable failing testcase. Lines 79–81 only check whether declared failures/errors are positive and reject with "else if (!caseFailed && !nested.length)"; they never reconcile failure counts. A focused invocation of retryRegressions with a failing check named `security` and a passing retry returned `[{"verdict":"flaky","blocking":false}]`. This behavior predates the change, but the requested security guarantee remains unmet.
candidates.suggestion: Represent security checks explicitly and preserve their blocking failure across retries; cover both targeted and full-retry paths.
candidates.failure_scenario: A security scan detects a vulnerability on its first run, then passes on retry; the gate reports flaky and permits the run to proceed.

candidates.title: A timed-out targeted retry can be classified as flaky
candidates.detail: A targeted retry that times out falls through to a full retry. If that full retry passes, the result is classified as a nonblocking flake, even though the targeted attempt did not pass. The request requires a full retry after a targeted pass and leaves timeout handling out of scope.
candidates.suggestion: Preserve the targeted timeout as a blocking result instead of allowing a subsequent pass to erase it.
candidates.failure_scenario: The original test check fails, its targeted retry times out, and the subsequent full check passes; the gate reports flaky and does not block.

candidates.title: A passing retry can clear a security check failure
candidates.detail: Retry classification treats every check alike: a passing full retry becomes a nonblocking flake. There is no guard for security checks, despite the request requiring that a security check failure never become a pass. This behavior existed in the full-retry path before the change, but the requested protection remains absent.
candidates.suggestion: Identify security checks using a trusted configuration or existing authoritative classification and keep their initial failure blocking on every retry path.
candidates.failure_scenario: A configured security check passes on baseline, fails after the change, and passes on its full retry; the comparison becomes nonblocking flaky.

candidates.title: Add the requested security-check retry test
candidates.detail: The retry matrix covers ordinary checks, timeouts, and confinement failures, but does not exercise a security check that fails initially and then passes on retry. The request explicitly requires verifying that such a failure cannot become a pass.
candidates.suggestion: Add a test that runs a failing security check through the relevant retry and classification path, makes the retry succeed, and asserts that the original security failure remains blocking.
candidates.failure_scenario: A security check fails on its first execution and succeeds on a later attempt; a future regression could classify it as a nonblocking flake without a test detecting the change.

candidates.title: Untrusted report timings can bypass the gate slot
candidates.detail: The decision to bypass the gate slot relies entirely on durations supplied by the JUnit report. The check under test can write that report, so it can claim a short duration for a file whose targeted retry runs for much longer. This lets candidate-controlled data steer the factory's shared concurrency limit.
candidates.suggestion: Base the slot bypass on a trusted measurement or otherwise enforce the duration bound during the targeted retry; treat untrusted report timings as insufficient to authorize bypass.
candidates.failure_scenario: A changed test writes a JUnit report naming one existing test file with time="0". Its targeted retry then runs a long workload outside the gate slot, despite the configured duration bound.

candidates.title: A failed security check can become a nonblocking flake
candidates.detail: The request says that “a security check's failure never becomes a pass.” The retry selection and classification do not distinguish security checks: any regressed check whose full retry passes is marked flaky and nonblocking.
candidates.suggestion: Identify security checks through trusted configuration or existing check metadata and preserve their blocking failure after any retry.
candidates.failure_scenario: A baseline security check passes, its post-change run fails, and its full retry passes. The comparison becomes flaky with blocking=false, allowing the change to proceed despite the original security failure.

candidates.title: Known failing files are not retried when output names a changed file
candidates.detail: The request states that a check with structured failure files should “retry only the failing test files.” The existing pointsAt exclusion still removes such failures before targeted retry selection. Test failure output commonly contains a changed test or source location, so these failures receive no confirmation retry.
candidates.suggestion: Apply the targeted retry rule to eligible structured test failures even when their output points at a changed file.
candidates.failure_scenario: A test check reports a failing file in JUnit and prints `changed.test.ts:12`, where that file is in the change. retryRegressions returns the original result without invoking the targeted runner.

candidates.title: Incomplete suite failure counts can be treated as a complete file list
candidates.detail: The request says “If the files can't be determined, fall back to today's full retry.” When a suite has no file attribute but reports failures, the parser accepts it if any child testcase failed, without checking whether all reported failures are represented. A partial report can therefore omit failing files and still trigger a targeted retry.
candidates.suggestion: Validate that suite failure and error counts are fully accounted for by identifiable child failures; otherwise treat the file list as unknown.
candidates.failure_scenario: A suite reports failures="2" but contains only one failed testcase with a file attribute. That file fails again alone, so the retry confirms a regression without running the other, unidentified failing file.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the initial TLS connection
findings.detail: The initial connection accepts any certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that connection. A man-in-the-middle can relay the pairing request to the real coordinator, return its code and secret to the worker, and present its own certificate. The owner sees the same code on both sides and approves it; the attacker then observes the claim and issued token. Pinning the attacker's certificate on subsequent requests does not prevent this. The submitted worker certificate fingerprint is never authenticated or used to bind the exchange.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to both endpoints' certificate fingerprints and the pairing exchange, so relaying through a different TLS certificate changes the code or causes verification to fail.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies the real coordinator's pairing response, and forwards the approved claim while terminating both TLS connections.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-27 sends the initial pairing request with only `{ signal }`; :39 subsequently pins `first.fingerprint`. src/workers/tls.ts:103 uses `rejectUnauthorized: false`, and :114 checks the certificate only when `options.pin !== undefined`. src/db/workers.ts:85-89 claims an approved token using only the pairing secret.
verification.trigger: An active intermediary terminates the initial TLS connection and relays the coordinator's pairing response and code. Owner approval lets the intermediary claim the token; the worker persists the intermediary's certificate fingerprint. The matching code does not authenticate the TLS endpoint.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
findings.detail: Private read protection is an in-memory registry. Pairing releases the token and fingerprint registrations on return, and `runWorker` registers them only in the worker CLI process. A daemon running gates or agents in a separate process therefore does not include those files in its sandbox deny paths. The coordinator TLS key has the same lifetime problem when its listener is disabled after the key has been created. Mode 0600 does not protect files from another process running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the configured worker credential and TLS key paths in every process that constructs agent or gate sandboxes, independent of whether a worker or listener is currently running.
findings.failure_scenario: Pair a worker, then run a factory daemon and a gate on the same machine; the daemon's sandbox is built without the worker token path registered, allowing a gate with access to that path to read the token.

verification.evidence: src/util/private-reads.ts:4 stores registrations in a process-local `Map`; :30 returns only that map's keys. src/workers/client.ts:55-57 releases pairing registrations. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 builds denies from `credentials` and `privateReadPaths()`; the built-in credential paths at :150-161 omit worker files.
verification.trigger: Pair a worker, then start a separate daemon. Its deny list lacks the worker credentials. A gate whose read allowances include the credential location—for example, a configured data directory outside the OS home—can read the token. The default home-wide gate deny protects the usual location but does not provide the required specific protection.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate creation permanently blocks restart
findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the final key path before invoking OpenSSL. If generation fails, times out, or the process stops before both files are complete, the next start either rejects the incomplete pair or tries to parse invalid material. No cleanup or recovery occurs, so the worker listener or pairing command continues to fail on every subsequent start.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files under temporary names, validate them, and publish them only after successful generation; clean up incomplete temporary material on failure.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped after creating the empty key file but before OpenSSL creates the certificate; every later listener start throws `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18 creates `writeFileSync(keyPath, "", { flag: "wx", mode: 0o600 })` before awaiting OpenSSL. On restart, src/workers/tls.ts:16-17 checks for either missing file and throws `new Error("Incomplete worker TLS material")` if either exists. The catch at :45-47 only calls `release()` and rethrows; it does not remove partial files.
verification.trigger: With workers.listen enabled, interrupt first-time certificate generation after key.pem is created but before cert.pem exists. Every subsequent startup fails until the partial material is repaired manually. The interruption window is unusual and limited to initial generation.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
findings.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins the certificate observed on that connection. The displayed code comes from the coordinator but is not bound to that certificate or to an authenticated exchange. An intermediary can relay the pairing request and code unchanged, obtain the pairing secret and issued token, and leave the worker pinned to the intermediary's certificate even though the owner compared matching codes.
findings.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to the coordinator certificate and pairing exchange so a relaying intermediary cannot obtain a usable token or substitute its certificate.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, forwards the request to the real coordinator, and relays its code. The owner approves the matching code; the attacker claims the token and the worker pins the attacker's certificate.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-27 makes the first request without a pin, :33 prints the returned code, :39 pins the observed first certificate, and :47 persists that fingerprint. src/workers/tls.ts:103 disables certificate authority validation. src/db/workers.ts:85-89 returns the approved token based solely on the secret hash.
verification.trigger: An active intermediary forwards the pairing request to the real coordinator and relays its code. The owner approves the matching code, while the intermediary learns the claim secret, obtains the token, and causes the worker to pin the intermediary's certificate.

findings.title: Permanent TLS and configuration errors are retried silently forever
findings.detail: The heartbeat loop catches every request exception and retries without a deadline or diagnostic. This includes a changed coordinator fingerprint and malformed coordinator URL, neither of which can be repaired by retrying. The worker remains running but never sends another heartbeat, and the owner receives no explanation.
findings.suggestion: Retry only transient transport failures with a bounded policy; propagate permanent validation and certificate-pin failures with their original reason.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing. Every heartbeat fails fingerprint validation, but the worker silently retries indefinitely instead of reporting that it must be paired again.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:114-115 rejects a changed certificate with `new Error("Coordinator certificate fingerprint changed")`. src/workers/client.ts:99-102 catches every request exception and returns `undefined`; :93 loops indefinitely and :106-107 sleeps with a delay capped at 10 seconds. Only HTTP responses below 500 terminate the loop (:104-105).
verification.trigger: The coordinator certificate changes after pairing, or the configured origin is invalid. Each heartbeat throws a permanent error that is discarded, leaving the worker silently retrying forever instead of reporting the necessary repair.

findings.title: Existing TLS key loses sandbox protection when the listener is disabled
findings.detail: The TLS key is registered with the sandbox deny list only when the listener starts. After a listener has created the key, restarting the daemon with workers.listen unset skips registration even though the key remains on disk. Agent sandboxes that can read that data directory can then read the coordinator's private key, contrary to the requirement that it be denied in every agent sandbox.
findings.suggestion: Register protection for existing worker TLS material independently of whether the listener is enabled, and retain it for the daemon lifetime.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the listener once, then disable it and restart the daemon with the data directory outside the default home deny paths. A subsequent agent can read worker-tls/key.pem.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:15–16: `if (!listen) return undefined;` precedes `certificate(join(paths.home, "worker-tls"))`. The key deny is registered only inside that function: src/workers/tls.ts:14: `const release = protectPrivateFile(keyPath);`. Editor denies incorporate that process-local registry at src/harness/read-policy.ts:190: `const denyRead = policySpellings([...credentials, ...privateReadPaths()], true, fs);`.
verification.trigger: Enable workers once, then disable the listener and restart. The retained key is never registered for sandbox protection; with the data directory outside other denied paths, an editor running as the same user can read worker-tls/key.pem despite mode 0600.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation prevents future startup
findings.detail: Certificate generation creates the final key path before running openssl, but its error path leaves partial files behind. A timeout, failed openssl invocation, or interruption can therefore leave only the empty key or other incomplete material. Every later start rejects the incomplete material, requiring manual cleanup.
findings.suggestion: Generate both files in temporary paths and publish them only after successful generation, cleaning up partial temporary files on failure.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon is interrupted after creating key.pem but before openssl writes cert.pem. Subsequent starts fail with `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

verification.evidence: src/workers/tls.ts:18 writes an empty key.pem before `await sh(...)` at :19. src/workers/tls.ts:17 throws `Incomplete worker TLS material` whenever only one TLS file exists. Error handling at :45-47 performs no filesystem cleanup. src/server/workers.ts:16 awaits `certificate(...)`, propagating this failure.
verification.trigger: Interrupt initial certificate generation between creating key.pem and writing cert.pem. Later listener starts repeatedly fail rather than completing generation; manual repair is required. This is a narrow first-start timing window.

findings.title: Credential read protection ends with the pairing process
findings.detail: The worker token and coordinator fingerprint are registered in an in-memory deny list only while `pairWorker` or `runWorker` holds them. Pairing releases both registrations before exiting, and a separately running daemon has its own deny list. Likewise, an existing coordinator TLS key is not registered when the listener is disabled. An agent sandbox created by that daemon therefore does not receive these paths as private-file denies.
findings.suggestion: Register persisted worker credential and TLS-key paths in every process that constructs agent sandbox policies, independently of whether pairing, the worker loop or the listener is currently running.
findings.failure_scenario: Pair a worker, exit the pairing command, and run an agent through a separate daemon using the same data directory: that daemon's private-file deny list does not contain the stored worker token or coordinator fingerprint.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:47-48 registers the persisted fingerprint and token, then :55-57 releases both registrations before pairing returns. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 uses a process-local map. src/harness/read-policy.ts:217 applies the home-wide deny only when `gate` is true; editor credential denies at :150-190 do not include worker files unless dynamically registered.
verification.trigger: After pairing exits, a separate daemon runs an editor agent using the same data directory. The worker token and coordinator fingerprint are absent from its private-file registrations and built-in credential denies, so the editor can read them under the normal editor read policy.

findings.title: Privacy probe masks the cross-process credential protection gap
findings.detail: The real-Seatbelt test creates the TLS material and registers both worker files in the same process that starts the gate, retaining all registrations throughout the probe. It consequently passes even if a daemon started separately after pairing has no credential paths in its in-memory deny list.
findings.suggestion: Add a real-Seatbelt probe that persists credentials, releases the pairing registrations, and launches the gate from an independently initialized daemon or process; cover an existing TLS key with the listener disabled as well.
findings.failure_scenario: The current implementation releases the registrations after pairing, yet this test retains them and reports all three files denied.

verification.evidence: test/workers.test.ts:266 retains registrations with `const protectedFiles = files.slice(1).map((p) => privateFile(p, "synthetic-private-file"));` until releases at lines 295–296, after running gates. Production src/workers/client.ts:55–57 instead executes `cert.release(); for (const release of held) release();` when pairing returns. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 uses a process-local `Map`, and lines 19–21 delete registrations on release. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 derives protection from `privateReadPaths()`; its static credential list does not include worker files.
verification.trigger: The privacy probe runs gates in the same process while explicitly retaining all registrations, so it passes without testing protection after pairing exits or from another factory process. It therefore masks the cross-process registration gap.

findings.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
findings.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that untrusted connection. An active intermediary can forward the request to the real coordinator, relay its code to the worker, and retain the returned pairing secret. The owner and worker see matching codes, but the intermediary can claim the approved token and the worker pins the intermediary's certificate.
findings.suggestion: Bind the human-compared code to both the coordinator certificate fingerprint and the pairing exchange, so relaying a coordinator response through a different TLS certificate changes the code.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies `/worker/pair` to the coordinator, and relays the real code. After the owner approves it, the attacker claims the worker token.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:23-28 sends the initial pairing request with only `{ signal }`; lines 35-39 subsequently pin `first.fingerprint`. src/workers/tls.ts:103 sets `rejectUnauthorized: false`, and lines 114-115 verify the certificate only when `options.pin !== undefined`. src/db/workers.ts:83-89 looks up `tokenHash(secret)` and returns the approved token without authenticating the worker certificate.
verification.trigger: An attacker intercepts initial pairing, forwards the request, and relays the coordinator's code and secret. Owner approval succeeds with matching codes; the attacker uses the observed secret to claim the worker token.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
findings.detail: `protectPrivateFile` maintains an in-memory registry. Pairing releases its registrations before exiting, and `runWorker` registers the files only in the worker process. A separately running daemon on the same machine does not receive those registrations when it constructs Claude or Codex sandbox policies, so its agents can read the persistent worker token and coordinator fingerprint. Mode 0600 does not protect them from agents running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every daemon process that launches agents, including when the worker is stopped, and cover separate-process sandbox behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine runs both a worker and a factory daemon under the same user. An agent launched by the daemon reads `<data>/worker/token` and impersonates that worker.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:87-88 protects credentials through `privateFile(...)`. src/workers/tls.ts:52 implements this with `protectPrivateFile(path)`. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 stores registrations in a process-local `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>()`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 builds denials from `credentials` and `privateReadPaths()`; its built-in credential list at lines 150-161 excludes `<data>/worker/`. Lines 217-218 apply the home-wide read restriction only to gates.
verification.trigger: A worker and daemon run as separate processes under the same user. The daemon never registers the worker's token path, so an editor agent can read the mode-0600 token using that user's permissions and impersonate the worker.

findings.title: Disabling the listener leaves its existing TLS key unprotected from agents
findings.detail: The TLS key is added to the process-local private-read registry only when the listener is enabled. After an owner removes `workers.listen` and restarts the daemon, the existing key remains on disk but is no longer included in agent sandbox deny paths. An agent running as the same user can read it, compromising the certificate trusted by already paired workers if the listener is later re-enabled.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent TLS key path independently of whether the listener is currently enabled, or securely remove and rotate the material when disabling it.
findings.failure_scenario: A coordinator previously enabled workers, then starts with the listener disabled. A tool-enabled agent reads `<data>/worker-tls/key.pem` before the listener is enabled again.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:15–16: `if (!listen) return undefined;` skips `certificate(join(paths.home, "worker-tls"))`, whose src/workers/tls.ts:14 calls `protectPrivateFile(keyPath)`. src/util/private-reads.ts:4 initializes protection as an in-memory `const privatePaths = new Map<string, number>();`; it does not survive daemon restarts.
verification.trigger: Restart with workers disabled after TLS material has been created. Unless another configured deny covers the data directory, a tool-enabled editor can read the retained private key before the listener is enabled again.

findings.title: Store untrusted heartbeat fields only after redaction
findings.detail: Heartbeat capabilities are serialized directly into SQLite. Several worker-controlled strings can contain coordinator credentials or private strings, but sanitization occurs only when listing workers. This leaves the unredacted values in persistent storage even though the trust-boundary rules require redaction before storage.
findings.suggestion: Redact and apply private-string policy to worker-supplied capability fields before persisting them, while preserving the fields needed for version matching.
findings.failure_scenario: A paired worker sends a coordinator credential or private string in `osVersion`; the value is written verbatim to the workers table.

verification.evidence: src/workers/protocol.ts:8 accepts `osVersion: z.string().max(128)`. src/server/workers.ts:43–46 parses the heartbeat then calls `workers.heartbeat(current, capabilities)`. src/db/workers.ts:143–144 persists it with `UPDATE workers SET last_heartbeat_at=?,capabilities=? WHERE name=? AND state='approved'` and `.run(this.now(), JSON.stringify(c), w.name)`, without redaction. `this.sanitize(...)` is applied later when listing workers (src/db/workers.ts:124), after persistence.
verification.trigger: An approved worker submits an otherwise valid heartbeat containing a credential or private string of at most 128 characters in osVersion; the coordinator stores that value verbatim in workers.capabilities.

findings.title: Worker credentials are not denied in the daemon's agent sandboxes
findings.detail: The request requires the worker token and coordinator fingerprint to be read-denied to gates. The deny registry is process-local, but pairing and the worker loop run as separate CLI processes from the daemon. Their registrations are also released when those commands exit. A daemon on the same machine therefore does not add these files to its agent sandbox deny lists; mode 0600 does not protect them from agents running as the same user.
findings.suggestion: Register the persistent worker credential paths in every daemon process that can launch agents and gates, including when the worker command is not running.
findings.failure_scenario: A machine is both a paired worker and a coordinator. An agent launched by its daemon reads the token under the worker data directory and uses it to impersonate the worker.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:55-57 releases pairing-time protections: `cert.release(); for (const release of held) release();`. src/util/private-reads.ts:4,13 maintains only a process-local registration map. src/harness/claude.ts:203-211 derives editor read denials from `writeRoots(...)`; src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 includes only built-in credentials and that process's `privateReadPaths()`, with no built-in worker credential paths.
verification.trigger: A paired machine also runs its coordinator daemon. Pairing registrations are released, and a separately running worker cannot register paths in the daemon. An editor agent launched by the daemon can read the persisted worker token and impersonate it.

findings.title: Disabling the listener removes protection for an existing TLS key
findings.detail: The request says the TLS key is read-denied in every agent sandbox. When the listener is disabled, startup returns before registering the previously generated key with the process-local deny registry. The key remains on disk, and editor sandboxes do not otherwise deny the worker TLS directory.
findings.suggestion: Register the existing key path for the daemon lifetime independently of whether the listener is enabled.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner disables workers after having enabled them, then starts a run. An editor agent can read the retained coordinator TLS private key.

verification.evidence: src/cli/daemon.ts:30 calls `startWorkerListener(factory.workers, factory.cfg.paths, factory.cfg.workers.listen)` before starting integrations. However, src/server/workers.ts:15 returns immediately when disabled, bypassing the key protection at src/workers/tls.ts:14: `const release = protectPrivateFile(keyPath);`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:190 derives editor denies from `credentials` and `privateReadPaths()`.
verification.trigger: Disable workers after an enabled deployment, restart, then start a run. An editor can read the retained coordinator TLS key when no independent deny covers its location; the default credential list does not include ~/.limitless/worker-tls.

findings.title: Interrupted certificate generation permanently blocks listener startup
findings.detail: The key file is created before openssl runs, but a failed or interrupted generation leaves it behind. The next start sees incomplete TLS material and throws instead of generating a certificate, so a transient failure prevents the daemon from starting whenever the worker listener is configured.

candidates.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the initial TLS connection
candidates.detail: The initial connection accepts any certificate, and the displayed code is supplied by that connection. A man-in-the-middle can relay the pairing request to the real coordinator, return its code and secret to the worker, and present its own certificate. The owner sees the same code on both sides and approves it; the attacker then observes the claim and issued token. Pinning the attacker's certificate on subsequent requests does not prevent this. The submitted worker certificate fingerprint is never authenticated or used to bind the exchange.
candidates.suggestion: Bind the owner-verified pairing code to both endpoints' certificate fingerprints and the pairing exchange, so relaying through a different TLS certificate changes the code or causes verification to fail.
candidates.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, proxies the real coordinator's pairing response, and forwards the approved claim while terminating both TLS connections.

candidates.title: Worker credentials are not denied to sandboxes in other processes
candidates.detail: Private read protection is an in-memory registry. Pairing releases the token and fingerprint registrations on return, and `runWorker` registers them only in the worker CLI process. A daemon running gates or agents in a separate process therefore does not include those files in its sandbox deny paths. The coordinator TLS key has the same lifetime problem when its listener is disabled after the key has been created. Mode 0600 does not protect files from another process running as the same user.
candidates.suggestion: Register the configured worker credential and TLS key paths in every process that constructs agent or gate sandboxes, independent of whether a worker or listener is currently running.
candidates.failure_scenario: Pair a worker, then run a factory daemon and a gate on the same machine; the daemon's sandbox is built without the worker token path registered, allowing a gate with access to that path to read the token.

candidates.title: Interrupted certificate creation permanently blocks restart

No cleanup or recovery occurs, so the worker listener or pairing command continues to fail on every subsequent start.

candidates.failure_scenario: The daemon is stopped after creating the empty key file but before OpenSSL creates the certificate; every later listener start throws `Incomplete worker TLS material`.

candidates.title: Pairing code does not authenticate the coordinator connection
candidates.detail: The initial pairing request accepts any TLS certificate, and the worker pins the certificate observed on that connection. An intermediary can relay the pairing request and code unchanged, obtain the pairing secret and issued token, and leave the worker pinned to the intermediary's certificate even though the owner compared matching codes.

candidates.failure_scenario: An attacker intercepts the worker's first connection, forwards the request to the real coordinator, and relays its code. The owner approves the matching code; the attacker claims the token and the worker pins the attacker's certificate.

Verifier: 10 candidates, 10 checked, 1 refuted.

findings.title: Treat a worker confinement failure as a terminal failure
findings.detail: A check reporting a confinement failure is rejected as an invalid result, which calls workers.fail. After the retry is exhausted, the LAN executor runs the gates locally and can return a pass. This converts a failed security check into a successful gate result.
findings.suggestion: Preserve confinement failures as a distinct terminal failure and propagate them through the gate result without retrying them into a pass.
findings.failure_scenario: Both worker attempts report a Seatbelt launch failure, but the local fallback executes successfully; the overall gate is reported as passing.

verification.evidence: src/workers/protocol.ts:65 rejects confinement reports: `.refine((r) => !r.confinementError && !launchFailure(r.output), "Worker confinement failed")`. src/server/workers.ts:131-133 routes rejection through `workers.fail(id, ...)`. src/db/workers.ts:260 retries or marks failed with `j.attempt < 2 ? "queued" : "failed"`. src/gates/lan.ts:73-89 handles that failure by executing locally, then `workers.complete(handle.id, run, true); return workers.sanitize(run);`, without preserving the confinement failure in the result.
verification.trigger: Both worker attempts report a Seatbelt launch failure; local execution passes. The returned GateRun passes, erasing the blocking confinement outcome.

findings.title: Do not discard failed checks received before an infrastructure failure
findings.detail: Check events from a worker are persisted and forwarded, but the final result is replaced by the next attempt or local fallback if that worker disconnects before posting its GateRun. A later pass therefore erases an already observed failing check, contrary to the requirement that infrastructure retries never turn a failing check into a pass.
findings.suggestion: Preserve and account for validated failing check results across attempts when producing the final gate outcome.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts a failing test check and loses its connection before posting the final result; the retry or local fallback passes, so the run receives a passing GateRun.

verification.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:68–72 copies stored events into the event stream, then returns only the final result: `events.push(...stored.slice(index));` and `if (job.state === "done" && job.result) return JSON.parse(job.result) as GateRun;`. Local fallback likewise returns its own outcome at src/gates/lan.ts:86–89: `const [run] = await Promise.all([execution.result, stream]); ... return workers.sanitize(run);`. Neither path merges earlier failed checks. src/gates/executor.ts:211–215 forwards check events to hooks but returns `result` unchanged.
verification.trigger: A worker posts a valid failing check event, then disconnects before submitting its GateRun. After retry or local fallback passes that check, the executor returns a passing GateRun despite the recorded failure, violating the explicit requirement that infrastructure retries never turn a failing check into a pass.

findings.title: Do not retry certificate pin failures indefinitely
findings.detail: The catch treats every workerRequest exception as a transient connection error. That includes an invalid coordinator URL or a changed pinned TLS fingerprint, so the worker silently retries forever instead of surfacing the security or configuration failure. The retry has no deadline.

findings.title: Accepting a passing final result can erase an already reported failure
findings.detail: Check events and the final GateRun are validated independently. The coordinator never compares an event with the corresponding final result, so a worker can report a failed check and then submit the same check as passing. The final passing result is returned to the pipeline even though the coordinator has already received evidence of failure.
findings.suggestion: Track check results by lease attempt and reject a final result that contradicts the events for that attempt, preserving failures as infrastructure failures or explicitly represented retries.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker posts a valid event for the requested test with ok=false, then posts a valid GateRun for the same SHA and command with ok=true and exitCode=0. The job completes successfully.

verification.evidence: src/server/workers.ts:125 validates events with `validCheck(request, event.data.result, event.data.phase)`; lines 130–136 independently validate the final run and call `workers.complete(id, result.data.run)`. src/db/workers.ts:290–291 writes `state='done',result=?` without comparing stored events. src/gates/lan.ts:72 returns that final result.
verification.trigger: A leased worker submits a valid failing check event, then a matching, schema-valid passing final result. The job completes as passing despite its recorded failure.

findings.title: Restart discards in-flight LAN retry jobs
findings.detail: Only baseline, initial, and rebase handles are eligible for reattachment. A shutdown during a timeout rerun or a baseline or regression retry leaves its durable LAN job running, but resume treats its handle as stale, cancels it, and enqueues another execution. This repeats work that had already been leased or completed and defeats durable reattachment for these gate executions.
findings.suggestion: Persist enough retry context to reattach the matching durable handle on resume, including timeout and targeted retry purposes.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator shuts down after a worker completes a regression-retry job but before the pipeline checkpoints its result. On restart, the completed handle is discarded and the retry is run again.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/gate-execution.ts:29–39 only reuses a handle when stage/round/purpose match and `["baseline", "initial", "rebase"].includes(purpose)`; otherwise it calls `cancelGateExecution(pending.handle, ...)` and clears the checkpoint. Restart enters the gates stage through `runGateExecution(ctx, "gates", "initial", ...)` (src/pipeline/engine.ts:1215), so a persisted regression-retry handle is discarded. The restart test explicitly asserts `expect(fresh.attaches).not.toContainEqual(handle)` and `expect(fresh.starts).toHaveLength(2)` for regression retries (test/gate-executor.test.ts:899–900).
verification.trigger: Coordinator restarts with a completed LAN regression-retry job whose result has not been checkpointed by the pipeline. Resume discards its persisted handle and starts initial gates again; if the regression recurs, it also repeats the retry instead of consuming the completed result.

findings.title: Local fallback can populate a LAN baseline cache entry
findings.detail: After infrastructure failures, the LAN executor returns a locally executed GateRun as an ordinary LAN result. The baseline cache key was selected as LAN before execution, so a passing fallback baseline is cached under that key. A later run can reuse it while its actual gates execute on a worker with a different environment, even though the cache distinguishes executors to avoid comparing results from different environments.
findings.suggestion: Do not cache a baseline produced by local fallback under the LAN executor key; propagate the actual execution environment or mark fallback results non-cacheable.
findings.failure_scenario: No worker is available for a baseline, so local fallback passes and is cached as LAN. A worker later becomes available and runs the change, while the pipeline reuses the local baseline as its worker baseline.

verification.evidence: src/gates/lan.ts:77-89 runs `local.start(request, controller.signal)`, then `workers.complete(handle.id, run, true)` and `return workers.sanitize(run)`. src/pipeline/engine.ts:550-551 selects the cache key from configuration: `executor: cfg.gateExecutor === "lan" && cfg.workers.repos.includes(ctx.repo.slug) ? "lan" : "local"`. At src/pipeline/engine.ts:574-577, `const fresh = await runBaseline()` is cached with `if (cacheableBaseline(fresh, gates)) store.putBaselineCache(key, fresh, ctx.run.id)`. src/gates/cache.ts:157-172 checks passing results and check identities, without checking execution provenance.
verification.trigger: With LAN configured for an opted-in repository, unavailable workers cause the baseline to fall back locally. A passing local result is stored under the LAN cache key. When a worker becomes available, change gates can run remotely while using that local baseline, including on subsequent cache hits, potentially misclassifying environment-dependent failures as regressions.

findings.title: Bound retries for job requests and propagate permanent failures
findings.detail: The shared request loop discards every transport error and retries indefinitely, including certificate fingerprint mismatches and other permanent errors. It also retries every server error without a deadline. Heartbeats can continue renewing a job while a bundle, event, result, or failure request is stuck in this loop, so the coordinator never expires the lease or falls back locally. Permanent connection errors also leave the worker silently retrying instead of reporting the cause.
findings.suggestion: Classify retryable transport and server errors, propagate permanent errors, and bound job-request retries so a failed job stops renewing its lease or reports its infrastructure failure.
findings.failure_scenario: The coordinator accepts heartbeats but repeatedly returns HTTP 500 for a job's result endpoint. The worker retries that result forever while heartbeats renew the lease, leaving the gate run pending indefinitely.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:139 uses `for (;;)`, and lines 150–158 return on 200, throw on statuses below 500, otherwise sleep and retry with only the delay capped: `delay = Math.min(delay * 2, 10_000)`. Line 233 awaits this loop for `/result`; `job.reported = false` occurs only afterward in `finally` (line 239). Heartbeats independently send `jobs: heldJobs()` (line 173). src/db/workers.ts:187–189 renews each held lease with `this.now() + this.times.lease`, so it never expires while these heartbeats succeed.
verification.trigger: Repeated HTTP 500 responses from the result endpoint while heartbeats continue succeeding cause unlimited result retries and lease renewals, keeping the gate pending without retrying another worker or falling back locally. This is an unusual trigger: ordinary listener exceptions are converted to HTTP 400 (src/server/workers.ts:138–139).

findings.title: Reject a final result that contradicts streamed check failures
findings.detail: Check events are validated and stored independently of the final GateRun. The final result is checked only against the requested names and commands, so a worker can first report a failing check and then submit a passing result for the same check. The coordinator accepts the pass even though it has already recorded evidence of a failure.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile the final result with the events from the current lease and reject contradictory outcomes as an infrastructure failure.

findings.title: Allow the Bun executable resolved by the verifier’s PATH
findings.detail: The read exception grants only process.execPath, which is the Bun running the daemon. A verifier normally invokes `bun test` through its inherited PATH, which can resolve to a different installation under a private read root. That executable remains denied, so the reported verifier failure can persist. The new smoke check also invokes process.execPath explicitly, so it can pass in this configuration without exercising the verifier’s actual command.
findings.suggestion: Resolve the Bun executable using the same PATH supplied to the verifier, validate its canonical path against the denied paths, and have the smoke check exercise `bun test` through that PATH.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon starts with `/opt/homebrew/bin/bun`, while the verifier’s PATH resolves `bun` to `~/.bun/bin/bun`; the sandbox allows the former and denies the latter, but the smoke probe passes using the former.

verification.evidence: src/harness/claude.ts:174 defaults `bunExecutable = process.execPath`; :225 grants `spellings([bunExecutable])`; :246 sets `allowRead: [...readable, ...bun]`. src/harness/scratch.ts:279 includes `homedir()` among denied roots. src/util/proc.ts:796 preserves inherited environment values (`env[k] = v`), including PATH. scripts/smoke.ts:744 and :755 explicitly execute `process.execPath`, bypassing PATH resolution.
verification.trigger: The daemon executable and PATH-selected Bun are distinct binaries, with the latter under the denied home directory. Verifier `bun test` cannot read that executable, while the smoke probe can pass using the daemon executable.

findings.title: Smoke probe bypasses the verifier's test-command wrapper
findings.detail: The probe invokes Bun by absolute path and sets confineReads to true. The production verification stage does not set confineReads, so it receives the configured slotted-command wrappers and normally runs `bun test` through them. Consequently, the smoke check can pass while the wrapper hangs or otherwise prevents a verifier from running tests—the failure this change also attempts to address through EPERM handling.
findings.suggestion: Run the live probe through the same verification invocation setup and command wrapper used by the pipeline, including invoking `bun test` as a verifier would.
findings.failure_scenario: A regression makes the slotted `bun test` wrapper wait indefinitely when the sandbox denies its socket connections, while direct execution of the Bun binary still succeeds. The smoke check reports a pass, but production verifiers remain unable to run tests.

verification.evidence: scripts/smoke.ts:744 launches `cmd: [${JSON.stringify(process.execPath)}, "test", ...]` directly. The probe sets `confineReads: true` (scripts/smoke.ts:761), which selects no wrappers: `opts.confineReads ? [] : (this.state.slottedCommands ?? [])` (src/pipeline/context.ts:846). Production verification invokes `role: "verify"`, `mode: "readonly"` without confineReads (src/pipeline/engine.ts:1721–1740), so configured wrappers apply.
verification.trigger: With slotted test commands configured, a wrapper socket regression can block production verifier tests while this direct-executable smoke probe still passes. The new probe does not exercise that path.

findings.title: Home-relative paths and file URLs bypass sanitization
findings.detail:
The sanitizer compares link destinations only against literal filesystem roots. A home-relative link such as the one in the request is left broken, and a file URL containing the absolute worktree path is published unchanged, including the owner's username. The direct check below returned both inputs unchanged.

Command: bun -e 'let s=await Bun.file("src/gates/publication.ts").text(); let f=new Function(s.slice(s.indexOf("export function sanitizePublication"),s.indexOf("/** Check both")).replace("export function","function").replace(/: string( \| undefined)?/g,"")+";return sanitizePublication")(); for(let x of ["[file](~/.limitless/work/run/a.ts)","[file](file:///Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts)","[/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)"]) console.log(f(x,"/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run","/Users/alice/.limitless"))'
Output:
[file](~/.limitless/work/run/a.ts)
[file](file:///Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts)
[/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)
findings.suggestion: Recognize home-relative paths and local file URLs before comparing them with the configured roots, and add cases for both forms.
findings.failure_scenario: A report contains [file](file:///Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts) or [file](~/.limitless/work/run/a.ts).

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:8 checks only `path === root || path.startsWith(`${root}/`)`; line 24 returns unchanged links with `if (result === path) return match;`. Both supplied forms remain unchanged when executing the sanitizer.
verification.trigger: A link destination prefixed with `file://` or `~/.limitless` does not match the absolute configured roots, leaving local paths in publication text.

If the destination is already relative, an absolute worktree path in the visible label is never visited by the bare-path matcher and is published with the owner's username. The direct check reported in the preceding finding returned [/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts](a.ts) unchanged.
findings.suggestion: Sanitize local paths in link labels as well as destinations while preserving ordinary relative links.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementer reports [/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts](a.ts), a relative link whose visible label contains the absolute worktree path.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:13 matches the entire Markdown link, including its label. Lines 21–24 process only the destination: `const path = angle ?? bare; ... if (result === path) return match;`.
verification.trigger: `[/Users/alice/.limitless/work/run/a.ts](a.ts)` has an unchanged relative destination, so the entire link retains its absolute label and exposes the local path.

findings.title: Recheck ownership inside the merge helper before each merge command
