Verifier: 8 candidates, 8 checked, 1 refuted.

findings.title: Key validation does not enforce the required owner and mode
findings.detail: The startup check accepts any regular file with the owner-read bit set and no group or world permission bits. It does not check the file's owner, and it accepts modes such as 0700 and 0400 despite requiring mode 0600. A file owned by another user can therefore pass the metadata check even when the daemon cannot read it, deferring failure until a configured repository first needs a token.
findings.suggestion: Check the file owner and enforce the requested mode and readability during configuration loading, with a clear startup error.
findings.failure_scenario: A key file owned by another user has mode 0600. Its metadata passes this check, but the daemon cannot read it and App-authenticated GitHub calls fail later.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:390 performs only `key = statSync(privateKeyPath)`; src/config.ts:394 checks `!key.isFile() || (key.mode & 0o077) !== 0 || !(key.mode & 0o400)`. Neither verifies effective readability. Actual reading occurs later at src/integrations/github-identity.ts:64: `readFileSync(app.privateKeyPath)`.
verification.trigger: A traversable path contains another user's mode-0600 key. An unprivileged daemon can stat it, so startup accepts it, but App operations subsequently fail to read it.

findings.title: Verify the key is readable by the factory at startup
findings.detail: The permission check inspects mode bits but does not check the file owner or whether the daemon can actually read the file. A mode-0600 key owned by another user passes configuration loading, then fails only when the first App operation tries to read it. The check also accepts modes such as 0400 and 0700 despite requiring mode 0600.
findings.suggestion: Verify the file belongs to the running user, is readable, and has the required mode before accepting the configuration.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured key is a regular mode-0600 file owned by another user. Startup succeeds, but every GitHub operation for an App repository later fails with `cannot read or sign with private key`.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:394 validates metadata only: `!key.isFile() || (key.mode & 0o077) !== 0 || !(key.mode & 0o400)`. src/integrations/github-identity.ts:64 reads the key later; lines 65–67 then report `cannot read or sign with private key`.
verification.trigger: A regular mode-0600 key belongs to another user and is unreadable by the daemon. Startup succeeds instead of refusing, and subsequent App GitHub calls fail.

findings.title: Key validation does not enforce the required mode or ownership
findings.detail: The mode check accepts owner execute bits, so a key with mode 0700 passes despite the required mode 0600. It also never checks that the file belongs to the process owner, so a mode-0600 file owned by another user can pass startup validation even when the daemon cannot read it. The failure then occurs later during token acquisition instead of at startup.
findings.suggestion: Validate the required file mode and ownership, and confirm the file is readable during startup.
findings.failure_scenario: Configure a regular private-key file with mode 0700, or a mode-0600 file owned by another user. Configuration loads instead of refusing with the key-file reason.

verification.trigger: Configure a regular key with mode 0700. Startup accepts its owner execute permission instead of enforcing the requested mode. An unreadable foreign-owned mode-0600 file also passes metadata validation.

findings.title: Key validation tests omit owner-only executable mode and ownership
findings.detail: The permission cases cover group and world bits but do not exercise a mode such as 0700 or a file owned by another user. Consequently they pass with the incomplete startup validation and do not catch the underlying key-file defect.
findings.suggestion: Add a regression case for mode 0700 and a controlled ownership or stat fixture for a key owned by another user, asserting startup refusal.
findings.failure_scenario: A change that checks only group and world permission bits while ignoring owner execute bits and file ownership passes the current key permission tests.

verification.evidence: test/github-app.test.ts:102 tests only `test.each([0o644, 0o640, 0o601])`; lines 103–104 chmod and assert rejection, without changing ownership. src/config.ts:394 checks `!key.isFile() || (key.mode & 0o077) !== 0 || !(key.mode & 0o400)`, which ignores owner execute bits and file ownership.
verification.trigger: A validator that accepts owner-executable keys (for example mode 0700) or ignores file ownership still passes the current permission tests, leaving those validation gaps undetected.

findings.title: An App key outside the config directory can be exposed to agents
findings.detail: The configuration accepts any absolute key path, but the agent read policy automatically denies the config directory, not the configured key file. A key placed in a repository checkout or another agent-readable location can therefore be read by an agent or gate despite the requirement that the key never reach them.
findings.suggestion: Restrict the key to a protected location or add its canonical path to every agent and gate read-deny policy, including aliases.
findings.failure_scenario: The operator configures `private_key_path` to a mode-0600 file in a checkout. An agent running as the same user can read that file through its permitted checkout access.

verification.evidence: src/config.ts:387 accepts `resolve(configDir, a.private_key_path)` without restricting location; src/config.ts:518 constructs `readPolicy: configureReadPolicy(raw.sandbox, configDir)`. src/harness/read-policy.ts:42 adds only configured denies and `configDir`: `denyRead: Object.freeze([...paths("deny_read"), configDir])`. src/harness/codex.ts:321–324 grants root read and checkout writes while denying only `denyRead`.
verification.trigger: Configure an owner-readable mode-0600 key inside an agent's checkout, outside existing denied paths, without an explicit sandbox deny. Startup accepts it and the same-user agent can read the private key.

findings.title: Manual landing bypasses the configured App identity
findings.detail: The request requires “one implementation used by every factory gh invocation for a repository” and says configured repositories use the App without fallback. findings.title: Older workers still consume rounds on authentication failure
findings.detail: The fallback depends entirely on the new failureClass field. A worker running the previous release does not emit that field, so its structured Claude authentication failure arrives as an ordinary error and is returned to the engine. The engine then commits the unchanged round and runs gates and verification, reproducing the issue during a coordinator-first rollout.
findings.suggestion: Negotiate worker capability or protocol version and avoid dispatching affected Claude sessions to workers that cannot report structured authentication failures.
findings.failure_scenario: A new coordinator dispatches an implementation to an older LAN worker whose OAuth token has expired; the old worker reports status error without failureClass, and the coordinator treats the round as completed.

verification.evidence: src/workers/agent-protocol.ts:31 accepts `failureClass: z.literal("authentication").optional()`. src/pipeline/lan-agent.ts:208–213 returns the worker result when `result.confinement?.ok !== false && result.status !== "cancelled" && result.failureClass !== "authentication"`. An older worker's ordinary error satisfies that condition. src/pipeline/engine.ts:1396–1401 records the error as `implementerIssue` and sets `implementationReadyRound = round`.
verification.trigger: A previous-release worker returns an authentication rejection as status error without failureClass. The coordinator accepts it as the implementation result and continues the round instead of running locally.

findings.title: New worker reports are rejected by older coordinators
findings.detail: The result schema was strict in the previous release. A new worker includes failureClass in an authentication failure report, so an older coordinator rejects the report as containing an unknown field. This breaks mixed-version operation and can leave the job failing instead of falling back locally.
findings.suggestion: Make protocol evolution compatible with older coordinators, for example through capability negotiation or a staged release that first permits unknown result fields.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker is upgraded before its coordinator and reports a Claude authentication failure with failureClass set; the older coordinator's strict AgentResultReport validation rejects it.

verification.evidence: src/workers/agent-protocol.ts:31 adds `failureClass: z.literal("authentication").optional()`. The base revision's AgentResultReport lacks that field and ends with `.strict()` (base src/workers/agent-protocol.ts:82). src/workers/client.ts:912–925 spreads `...result` into the report and posts it without compatibility filtering. src/server/workers.ts:249 validates incoming reports with `AgentResultReport.parse(body)`.
verification.trigger: An upgraded worker sends an authentication result containing failureClass to a coordinator running the previous release. Its strict schema rejects the unknown field, so the worker's result cannot be accepted.

findings.title: Authentication fallback can follow adoption of a partial worker commit
findings.detail: Authentication errors can occur after earlier model turns and tool calls, but the parser classifies them identically to a login rejection before the session. The worker publishes any changes before reporting the result, and this path adopts that commit before falling back locally. Consequently the local implementer runs on top of partial work from the failed session, and that work is already published even if the local invocation also fails.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish a rejection before any session work from an authentication failure after work began, and handle partial work without treating the session as one that never ran.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker implementer edits files during an initial successful turn, then its token expires on a later API call. The worker publishes the edits, the coordinator adopts them, and an authentication fallback starts a local implementer against that partial commit.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:905 calls `publishAgentChanges(...)` after the harness result without excluding authentication failures. src/workers/publication.ts:86 commits changed files with `commitAll(...)`. src/pipeline/lan-agent.ts:201 executes `await publication?.adopt(sha, request as AgentPublication)` before checking authentication at line 211 and calling `return fallback(id)` at line 217.
verification.trigger: A worker changes files before a later API call rejects authentication. Its partial changes are published and adopted before the local implementation starts, so the fallback runs against the partial worker commit rather than the original parent.

findings.title: Treating every authentication error as a startup failure can replay completed work
findings.detail: The parser marks an authentication error regardless of whether the session has already made successful model calls or executed tools. The LAN executor then adopts the worker commit and runs the same round locally, while coordinator routing can also start another candidate. A token that expires during a multi-turn session can therefore cause completed edits or other tool side effects to be repeated, even though the worker did run the session.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish an authentication rejection before any session work from one after successful turns or tool calls, and only use the startup fallback for the former.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker edits files in a successful first turn, then receives a 401 on a later API call. Its commit is adopted and the implement prompt is run again locally against that changed checkout.

findings.title: Lifecycle transitions can disappear between polls
findings.detail: Comments are derived from the current run status, and an event is persisted only when reconciliation observes that status. A run that enters needs_human and is resumed or resolved before the next poll never records or posts that event. Likewise, a second needs_human episode is suppressed by the first episode's done checkpoint. This does not provide a durable side effect for each transition across restarts or polling intervals.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when transitions occur, with an identity for each status episode, and reconcile those records independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resumes it before the next queue poll; no needs-you comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:97–102 reads `run = store.getRun(snapshot.id)` and adds the event only `if (run.status === "needs_human")`. Lines 112–114 skip absent events unless already pending: `if (!events.has(event) && state(effect) !== "pending") continue;`.
verification.trigger: A run enters and leaves needs_human between polls, before its comment becomes pending. Reconciliation never posts the required needs-you reason.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates only run for queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Both the reconciler and its timer are conditional on the issue queue's repository and trusted-account configuration. Runs started through CLI, MCP, or GitHub triggers in any other configured repository therefore receive no lifecycle labels or comments, even though the requested behavior covers every start path and does not require queue admission to be enabled.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and select linked issues according to the supported repository settings.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository has the GitHub integration configured but is absent from githubQueue.repos; a CLI run with `Closes #42` produces no lifecycle updates.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12 defines lifecycleManaged using `cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; line 43 skips with `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:144 also returns immediately when queue repositories or trusted accounts are absent.
verification.trigger: A CLI run contains Closes #42 in a GitHub-integrated repository outside githubQueue.repos. Its required lifecycle labels and comments are skipped.

findings.title: A partial failure can release an issue before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: The label loop removes in-progress before adding failed. If the add fails, reconciliation logs the failure and queue selection continues in the same poll. The existing latest-run admission check only finds issue-source runs, so it does not protect a failed CLI or MCP run linked through its prompt. The issue can be selected again using its old priority approval before the failed label is retried.
findings.suggestion: Keep admission closed until the failure transition is durably reflected, including for prompt-linked runs; order label writes so a partial transition does not release the issue.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #42` fails; deleting in-progress succeeds but adding failed returns an error. The same poll sees the old priority label and starts a queue run without re-approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:13 orders labels as in-progress, needs-you, failed; lines 68–86 delete non-target labels before adding failed and catch write failures at lines 93–95. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 continues into admission after reconciliation. src/db/store.ts:1268 restricts latestIssueRun to `json_extract(runs.source_ref, '$.kind') = 'issue'`, excluding ordinary CLI Closes runs.
verification.trigger: An otherwise eligible issue's CLI run fails. Removing in-progress succeeds but adding failed fails. The failed run no longer claims the issue, and latestIssueRun excludes it, so the same poll can admit a queue run using the old approval.

findings.title: An older run can overwrite a newer run's issue labels
findings.detail: The latest-run map is computed once before any GitHub requests. If another run for the issue is created while a label request is awaiting, the old run remains designated latest and can complete its label transition after the newer run starts. Its completed cursor then prevents correction until the newer run is reconciled on a later poll.
findings.suggestion: Recheck which run owns the issue after awaited operations and before each label mutation and completion checkpoint.
findings.failure_scenario: While reconciliation fetches labels for a failed run, a new run for the same issue starts; the old reconciliation then applies failed and removes in-progress for the active run.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:35–39 builds `latest` once from `store.issueLifecycleRuns()`. Line 56 checks that snapshot before awaiting the labels request at line 60. Lines 63–71 subsequently re-read only `store.getRun(snapshot.id)` and its desired label; they never recheck whether a newer run owns the issue.
verification.trigger: A newer run for the issue is created while the old failed run's labels request is awaiting GitHub. The old reconciliation can then remove in-progress and apply failed despite the newer active run, until a later poll corrects it.

findings.title: Persist lifecycle events when they occur, not only when a poll observes them
findings.detail: The needs-human, failure, and cancellation comments are created only when reconciliation observes the corresponding current status. No pending effect exists until the comment loop reaches that event. A status that changes between polls, or while an earlier comment write is failing, is therefore never recorded or retried. The single done cursor also suppresses a second needs-human episode for the same run.
findings.suggestion: Record each lifecycle event and its publication-safe content durably at the state transition, then let polling deliver each recorded event.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next poll; reconciliation sees the resumed status and never posts the required reason. Similarly, a failed started-comment write can delay processing until after needs_human has ended.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:99–103 derives comment events from current status. Lines 159–161 persist an event only when its comment is reached. The ordered loop at line 110 processes started first, and lines 165–167 execute `failure(error); break;` on a write failure.
verification.trigger: A needs_human episode ends before polling observes it, or a failed started-comment write prevents reaching its needs_human comment before the run resumes. No durable needs_human event exists, so its required reason is permanently omitted. This overlaps C1.

findings.title: Reconcile issue-linked runs outside queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle processing is restricted to repositories listed in githubQueue with a nonempty trusted list, and the reconciler is started only when that queue is enabled. The request applies lifecycle updates to issue-linked runs from every start path; it does not condition those updates on queue admission being enabled for the repository.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and determine the target repository from each linked issue.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts a run with Closes #12 in a repository not listed in githubQueue, or with the queue disabled. No lifecycle labels or new lifecycle comments are written for that issue.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:10–12 requires `cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length` and membership in `cfg.githubQueue.repos`; line 43 skips other repositories: `if (!lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) continue;`. src/integrations/index.ts:66–67 starts reconciliation only when `!!queue?.repos.length && !!queue.trusted.length`.
verification.trigger: A new owner-started run contains Closes #12, but its repository is outside githubQueue or queue configuration is disabled. The required lifecycle labels and comments are never reconciled.

findings.title: Prevent re-pick while a failed label write is pending
findings.detail: The new re-approval guard depends on the failed label being visible on GitHub. If that write fails, the queue continues selection in the same poll. The existing latestIssueRun lookup only considers issue source references, so it cannot supply a local failure guard for runs linked through a Closes directive.
findings.suggestion: Use the existing admission and claim check to account for the latest linked run and its failure while the GitHub failure-label effect is pending.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with Closes #12 fails, the GitHub failed-label POST fails, and issue #12 still has its previously trusted priority label. latestIssueRun returns no issue-sourced run, so the queue can immediately select the issue again without re-approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:93-95 catches label-write errors with "failure(error)" and continues. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 then proceeds from reconciliation to candidate selection, supplying "latest: factory.store.latestIssueRun(repo, issue.number)" at line 223. src/db/store.ts:1268 restricts that lookup to "json_extract(runs.source_ref, '$.kind') = 'issue'"; issueClaim at lines 1224-1229 considers only active statuses.

findings.title: Authenticate the comment used as a delivery checkpoint
findings.detail: A pending comment is considered delivered when any issue comment contains the predictable marker. The code does not verify the comment author or exact body, although issue comments are untrusted data. A third party can therefore make the reconciler mark a failed write as done without the factory ever posting the required comment.
findings.suggestion: Verify that a matching comment was authored by the configured factory identity and matches the recorded body before marking the effect complete.
findings.failure_scenario: After a comment POST fails and leaves its effect pending, another issue participant posts a comment containing the run's lifecycle marker. On the next poll the factory treats that comment as its own and permanently skips the real update.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:121–130 reads pending comments using `z.object({ body: z.string() })` and accepts `comments.some((c) => c.body.includes(marker))`, then calls `save(effect, "done")`. No author identity is checked.
verification.trigger: A comment POST fails, leaving its effect pending. Another participant posts the lifecycle marker. The next poll marks delivery complete and permanently suppresses the factory's comment.

findings.title: Lifecycle events can disappear between polls
findings.detail: The reconciler derives needs-human and failure comments only from the current run status. If a run enters one of those states and is resolved or restarted before the next poll, no pending effect was recorded, so that event is never published. The pending-comment tests cover a status change only after a poll has already attempted the comment; they do not cover a transition entirely between polls.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the transitions occur, and add a test that enters needs_human or failed and leaves it before reconciliation runs.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll. The issue receives no needs-you comment or label for that event.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102 creates the event only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; line 113 skips it when `!events.has(event) && state(effect) !== "pending"`. src/db/store.ts:2038 changes resolved runs to `status: "resolved"`.
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and is resolved before reconciliation observes it. No pending checkpoint exists, so subsequent polls omit the needs-you comment and label.

findings.title: Encoded credentials can reach public issue comments
findings.detail: The comment body is passed directly to literal credential redaction. The private-string check detects encoded private-string entries, but registered credentials are not necessarily entries in that list. A credential encoded in a run error can therefore be published in a form a reader can decode.
findings.suggestion: Decode supported representations before credential redaction, or reject comment text containing encoded registered credentials before publication.
findings.failure_scenario: A failed run's error contains a percent-encoded registered token that is absent from private-strings.txt; the posted failure comment contains the encoded token.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:134–148 passes the reason directly through `redactCredentials(...)` and checks only `loadPrivateStrings(...)` before posting at line 163. src/util/proc.ts:1234–1236 registers literal and JSON-escaped credential variants, without percent decoding. src/gates/private.ts:120–122 loads private entries solely from file lines.
verification.trigger: A failure reason contains a percent-encoded registered credential whose literal value is absent from private-strings.txt. Literal credential matching misses it, the private-string check passes, and the recoverable credential is persisted and posted publicly.

findings.title: An unrelated comment can satisfy a pending publication checkpoint
findings.detail: Retry reconciliation trusts a marker found in any issue comment without checking its author or body. Issue comments are untrusted input, so a commenter who knows a run ID can make the factory record an effect as completed even though the factory never posted it.
findings.suggestion: Verify the comment belongs to the expected GitHub identity and matches the saved publication body before marking the effect done.
findings.failure_scenario: A user posts the predictable failed-event marker, and the factory's subsequent comment POST fails before reaching GitHub. On the next poll, the user's marker causes the pending failure comment to be marked done.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:120 constructs `<!-- limitless-lifecycle:${run.id}:${event} -->`; lines 128–130 accept any comment containing that marker as completion. Lines 159–163 persist `save(effect, "pending")` before attempting the POST.
verification.trigger: A participant preposts the predictable failed-event marker, then the factory's POST fails before publication. On retry, the unrelated comment satisfies the pending checkpoint and the failure notification is permanently skipped. This is the same underlying defect as C9.

findings.detail: The lifecycle reconciler skips repositories outside githubQueue.repos, and it is not started when the issue queue is disabled. The request requires updates for runs started through CLI, MCP, label, and comment paths as well as the queue; those paths can target repositories that are not configured for automatic issue selection.

verification.trigger: A CLI run containing Closes #123 targets a repository outside githubQueue.repos. Reconciliation skips all lifecycle labels and comments despite the explicit any-start-path requirement.

findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #7` starts in a repository with no issue-queue configuration; no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

findings.title: Transient lifecycle events are lost between polls
findings.detail: The request requires each label change and comment to be a recorded side effect with a durable checkpoint. Here needs-human, failed, and cancelled events are discovered only from the current status. If a run enters and leaves one of those states before a poll observes it, no effect is recorded and its comment is permanently lost. The initial in-progress label can likewise be skipped if the run reaches a later state before its first poll.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the corresponding transitions occur, then reconcile each recorded effect independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll; the reconciler never posts the needs-you reason or applies its label.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:101–102 only creates the event when `run.status === "needs_human"`; line 113 skips absent events unless their checkpoint is already pending. src/db/store.ts:2037–2038 permits needs_human to become resolved: `(opts.from ?? verification.trigger: A run reaches needs_human and is resolved before the next lifecycle poll. Although same-run resumption is not supported, this supported transition likewise loses the needs-you label and reason because no event was checkpointed.

findings.title: A failed label write can allow a failed CLI issue to be picked
findings.detail: A lifecycle write failure is caught and queue selection continues, but `latestIssueRun` only finds runs with an issue source reference. findings.suggestion: Include all linked-issue runs in the existing eligibility/admission evidence, including runs linked through their prompt.
findings.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #7` fails, the GitHub failed-label write errors, and the issue still has its previously approved priority label; the same poll can create a queue run for it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:191 awaits reconciliation before querying issues. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:93-95 logs label-write errors and continues. findings.title: Re-approval in the same timestamp second is rejected
findings.detail: The requirement specifies the labeled events' order and actor. Comparing parsed timestamps with strict greater-than rejects a trusted priority event that follows the failure event but has the same timestamp precision, even though the timeline preserves their order.
findings.suggestion: Use the ordered timeline events to determine whether a trusted priority application follows the failure event, including ties in timestamps.
findings.failure_scenario: GitHub records the failure label and a subsequent trusted priority label with the same second in `createdAt`; the issue remains ineligible.

candidates.failure_scenario: A future change loses a failed comment after the failed label is written and the daemon restarts; the existing restart test still passes because it covers only the started event.

candidates.title: Encoded credentials can reach public issue comments
candidates.detail: The comment body is passed directly to literal credential redaction. The private-string check detects encoded private-string entries, but registered credentials are not necessarily entries in that list. A credential encoded in a run error can therefore be published in a form a reader can decode.
candidates.suggestion: Decode supported representations before credential redaction, or reject comment text containing encoded registered credentials before publication.
candidates.failure_scenario: A failed run's error contains a percent-encoded registered token that is absent from private-strings.txt; the posted failure comment contains the encoded token.

candidates.title: An unrelated comment can satisfy a pending publication checkpoint
candidates.detail: Retry reconciliation trusts a marker found in any issue comment without checking its author or body. Issue comments are untrusted input, so a commenter who knows a run ID can make the factory record an effect as completed even though the factory never posted it.
candidates.suggestion: Verify the comment belongs to the expected GitHub identity and matches the saved publication body before marking the effect done.
candidates.failure_scenario: A user posts the predictable failed-event marker, and the factory's subsequent comment POST fails before reaching GitHub. On the next poll, the user's marker causes the pending failure comment to be marked done.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to configured queue repositories
candidates.detail: The lifecycle reconciler skips repositories outside githubQueue.repos, and it is not started when the issue queue is disabled. The request requires updates for runs started through CLI, MCP, label, and comment paths as well as the queue; those paths can target repositories that are not configured for automatic issue selection.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and cover all repositories for which linked runs can be created.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #123` targets a configured repository outside githubQueue.repos; it receives no lifecycle labels or comments.

candidates.title: A removed priority label can satisfy re-approval
candidates.detail: The post-failure check accepts any historical trusted priority application, even when that label is no longer present. The separate approved-label check can be satisfied by a different priority label that predates the failure, so the two checks together do not establish that a current priority label was re-applied after failure.
candidates.suggestion: Require the post-failure event to be the latest trusted application of a currently present approved priority label.
candidates.failure_scenario: An issue retains priority:2 from before failure. A trusted user applies and then removes priority:1 after failure; the historical priority:1 event permits the issue to be picked using the stale priority:2 label.

candidates.title: Lifecycle updates are limited to queue-configured repositories
candidates.detail: The request covers “any start path: queue, `limitless run` with `Closes #n`, MCP, label or comment trigger.” Reconciliation skips repositories outside `githubQueue.repos`, and the reconciler is not started at all when the queue is disabled. Consequently, runs started through those other paths receive no lifecycle labels or the required comments unless their repository also happens to be configured for the issue queue.
candidates.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission and apply it to linked issues from all supported start paths.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run with `Closes #7` starts in a repository with no issue-queue configuration; no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

candidates.title: Transient lifecycle events are lost between polls
candidates.detail: The request requires each label change and comment to be a recorded side effect with a durable checkpoint. Here needs-human, failed, and cancelled events are discovered only from the current status. If a run enters and leaves one of those states before a poll observes it, no effect is recorded and its comment is permanently lost. The initial in-progress label can likewise be skipped if the run reaches a later state before its first poll.
candidates.suggestion: Record lifecycle events durably when the corresponding transitions occur, then reconcile each recorded effect independently of the current status.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and is resumed before the next queue poll; the reconciler never posts the needs-you reason or applies its label.

candidates.title: Repeated needs-human episodes share one comment checkpoint
candidates.detail: The comment effect is keyed only by run and event name. Once `comment:needs_human` is done, a later needs-human transition in the same resumed run is suppressed, including its new reason. The request requires a comment when a run reaches needs_human, and the second episode is a distinct transition.
candidates.suggestion: Key lifecycle effects by a durable transition or status-episode identifier.
candidates.failure_scenario: A run asks for human help, resumes after an answer, then needs human help again for a different reason; only the first reason is posted.

candidates.title: A failed label write can allow a failed CLI issue to be picked
candidates.detail: A lifecycle write failure is caught and queue selection continues, but `latestIssueRun` only finds runs with an issue source reference. A failed CLI or MCP run linked through `Closes #n` has no such reference. Until the failed label is successfully written, the queue therefore sees neither the failure label nor that latest failed run and can select the issue without re-approval.
candidates.suggestion: Include all linked-issue runs in the existing eligibility/admission evidence, including runs linked through their prompt.
candidates.failure_scenario: A CLI run for `Closes #7` fails, the GitHub failed-label write errors, and the issue still has its previously approved priority label; the same poll can create a queue run for it.

candidates.title: Re-approval in the same timestamp second is rejected
candidates.detail: The requirement specifies the labeled events' order and actor. Comparing parsed timestamps with strict greater-than rejects a trusted priority event that follows the failure event but has the same timestamp precision, even though the timeline preserves their order.
candidates.suggestion: Use the ordered timeline events to determine whether a trusted priority application follows the failure event, including ties in timestamps.
candidates.failure_scenario: GitHub records the failure label and a subsequent trusted priority label with the same second in `createdAt`; the issue remains ineligible.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: Lifecycle reconciliation only runs when the issue queue has trusted accounts and only processes repositories listed in that queue. Consequently, CLI, MCP, label-triggered, and comment-triggered runs against other repositories receive no lifecycle labels or durable lifecycle comments, even though the request covers any start path.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and include all repositories with linked issues.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository is configured for GitHub integration but not in githubQueue.repos; `limitless run` with `Closes #7` starts and no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:11–13 defines lifecycleManaged as `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length && cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`. Lines 109–110 observe only issues passing that guard, and line 116 filters delivery through it.
verification.trigger: A CLI run containing `Closes #7` targets a repository outside githubQueue.repos; no lifecycle labels or start comment are delivered.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both event bodies always contain only a UI link and never inspect the run's reason. The fixed message is required as a fallback when publication checks block the reason, but this code uses it for every run. The new tests explicitly assert that the original reason is absent.
findings.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after credential redaction and private-string checking, falling back to fixed text when it cannot be published.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with `error: "tests failed"`; the issue receives only `failed: see ...` and the owner cannot see the requested reason in the comment.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82–83 constructs only `needs you: see ${link}.` and `failed: see ${link}.`; line 95 embeds that fixed text in the comment without the run's reason.
verification.trigger: A run fails with the publishable error `tests failed`; its failure comment contains the UI link but omits the required reason.

findings.title: A blocked comment is marked done without posting the required fallback
findings.detail: If the publication check rejects a comment, the effect is permanently marked done instead of creating and delivering a fixed safe message. The same suppression happens during the delivery-time recheck. This loses the lifecycle notification permanently.
findings.suggestion: Construct and check a fixed safe fallback and retain a pending effect until it is delivered.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string matches the generated run link or run ID; the start comment is marked done and no comment is ever posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:93–100 calls `checkBody(...)`, then on rejection executes `save(effect, "done")` and logs the error. Line 87 skips effects already recorded: `if (effects.has(effect)) continue;`. No fallback body is posted.
verification.trigger: A private string matches the run ID or UI link in a generated comment; the comment is permanently marked done without posting the required fixed fallback.

findings.title: Lifecycle transitions between polls are lost
findings.detail: The poller derives events solely from the current run status and records no transition at the point the status changes. A needs-human or failure state that is resolved before the next poll is never observed, so neither its comment nor its corresponding label is applied. A single effect key per event also prevents a second needs-human episode from producing a comment.
findings.suggestion: Persist lifecycle events with the state transition and reconcile those durable records on subsequent polls.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and the owner resolves it before the next queue poll; the issue never receives the needs-you update or reason.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82 creates needs_human comments only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; lines 105–110 observe current run snapshots. src/db/store.ts:2083–2088 updates the current row and publishes it without recording lifecycle effects. src/integrations/github-notifier.ts:299 suppresses its subscriber comments for managed issues.
verification.trigger: A managed run enters needs_human and is resolved before the next lifecycle poll; reconciliation sees only resolved and never records or delivers the needs-you label or comment.

duplicates.title: Transient lifecycle states are lost between polls
duplicates.detail: The reconciler creates effects only from the current run snapshot. It does not durably record a needs-human transition when it happens, so a transition that is resolved or resumed before the next poll produces neither the required comment nor its label change. This also affects transitions while the daemon is stopped.
duplicates.suggestion: Persist lifecycle events at the corresponding state transitions, then let polling deliver their checkpointed effects.
duplicates.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human and an owner resumes it before the next queue poll; the issue never receives the needs-you update.

findings.title: A failed issue can be picked before the failure label is applied
findings.detail: When the failed label is absent, eligibility falls back to accepting any trusted priority event after the run finished. If the lifecycle label write fails, that approval can occur before the failure label exists, yet the next queue poll can select the issue. This violates the required ordering after the failure label was applied.
findings.suggestion: Keep failed runs ineligible until the failure label application is observed and a trusted priority event follows it.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, adding `limitless:failed` fails, and a trusted user reapplies priority before the next poll. The issue has no failed label, so the timestamp fallback admits it without a priority event after the failure label.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:117–124 requires failure-label ordering only when `context.latest.status === "failed" && failed`; otherwise it accepts a trusted priority event with `Date.parse(e.createdAt) > context.latest.finishedAt`. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:227–234 catches a label-write failure, calls `logFailure(...)`, and continues. Queue selection then proceeds after reconciliation (src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:203–207).
verification.trigger: The run fails, in-progress is successfully removed (or absent), and adding limitless:failed fails. A trusted priority application after finishedAt lets admission accept the issue while limitless:failed is absent, without approval after the failure-label application.

findings.title: Failure and needs-you comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both terminal comments always use a fixed UI reference and never include the run's reason. The request requires a comment with the reason, using a fixed message when the private-strings check blocks that text. The added tests explicitly assert that the reason is absent.
findings.suggestion: Build these comments from the recorded reason, redact and check it, and use the fixed message only when publication is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with an ordinary, publishable error such as "tests failed"; the issue receives only "failed: see ..." and its watchers cannot see the reason.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82–83 sets `needs you: see ${link}.` and `failed: see ${link}.`; line 95 builds the posted comment solely from that text and the run ID.
verification.trigger: A failed or needs_human run has an ordinary publishable reason; watchers receive only a UI-link comment, with the required reason omitted.

findings.title: Publication errors permanently discard comments
findings.detail: Any exception while preparing or checking a comment marks the effect done. This includes transient inspection errors as well as a private-string match, so no later poll retries it and the required fixed fallback is never posted. The same permanent suppression occurs when rechecking a pending body at line 248.
findings.suggestion: Post a checked fixed fallback for a private-string match, and leave unexpected inspection failures pending for a later retry.
findings.failure_scenario: A private string matches the generated UI link, or the private-strings file is temporarily unreadable; the lifecycle event is recorded as done without any issue comment and remains absent after the condition is corrected.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:87: `if (effects.has(effect)) continue;`; :98-100: `catch (error) { save(effect, "done"); logFailure(run, repo, number, error); }`. Publication failures permanently checkpoint the comment as done instead of posting a fixed fallback or retrying.
verification.trigger: A private string matches the UI link, or loading private strings throws. The comment is marked done without posting and remains absent after the condition is corrected.

findings.title: A failed label write permits re-pick based on an earlier approval
findings.detail: When the failed label is absent, admission falls back to any trusted priority event after the run finished. Lifecycle write failures are explicitly nonfatal, so a failed label write can leave that branch active even though approval occurred before the failure label was applied. The next queue scan can therefore start another run without the required approval after the label.
findings.suggestion: Keep a failed run ineligible until the failure label has been observed and a trusted priority application is observed after that label.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, the owner reapplies a priority label, and posting `limitless:failed` fails. The same or a later poll sees the post-finish priority event and selects the issue despite there being no post-failure-label approval.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:117–124 branches on `context.latest.status === "failed" && failed`; when the failed label is absent, `events.some(...)` accepts a trusted priority event after finishedAt. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:227–234 logs label-write failures and continues; src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:265–269 reuses this same eligibility check for admission.
verification.trigger: A trusted owner reapplies priority after the run finishes but before limitless:failed is successfully applied. With no in-progress label remaining and the failed-label write unsuccessful, the timestamp fallback approves another run using that earlier approval.

findings.title: Lifecycle events between polls are never recorded
findings.detail: Reconciliation derives comments solely from the current run snapshot. A status entered and left between polls has no durable event recorded, so its required label and comment cannot be recovered on a later poll or restart.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle transitions durably when they occur and reconcile the recorded effects independently of the current status.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters `needs_human` and is resolved before the next issue queue poll. Reconciliation observes only `resolved`, so it never posts the needs-you comment or applies its label.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82: `if (run.status === "needs_human") events.set("needs_human", ...)`; :105: `const runs = store.issueLifecycleRuns();`. src/db/store.ts:2113: `buildUpdate({ ...opts.patch, status: "resolved" }, RUN_PATCH_COLUMNS)`. Reconciliation derives events from current run status rather than transition history.
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and is resolved before reconciliation observes it. The needs-you comment and label are never recorded or delivered.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to queue-enabled repositories
findings.detail: The reconciler only manages repositories listed in `githubQueue` with trusted accounts, and it is started only when that queue is enabled. The requested updates cover runs started by CLI, MCP, labels and comments as well as the queue, with GitHub App or gh identity depending on repository coverage.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation for linked issues independently of whether automatic queue admission is enabled for their repository.
findings.failure_scenario: An owner starts `limitless run` with `Closes #7` in a configured repository that is not in `githubQueue.repos`; no lifecycle labels or comments are sent for issue 7.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:11-13: `lifecycleManaged` requires `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length` and `cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; :110: `if (lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)) observe(run, repo, number);`; :116 filters delivery through the same predicate. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:156 also returns immediately when the queue is disabled.
verification.trigger: An owner starts a CLI run containing Closes #7 in a configured repository outside githubQueue.repos. No lifecycle labels or comments are produced for that issue.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both comments use fixed text even when the run has a safe, available reason. The request requires a comment with the reason, with a fixed fallback only when publication checks block that text.
findings.suggestion: Capture the reason in the durable event body, redact and check it, and use fixed fallback text when the check blocks it.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails with error "tests failed"; the issue receives only "failed: see <UI link>" and does not tell watchers why it failed.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82-83: `events.set("needs_human", `needs you: see ${link}.`)` and `events.set("failed", `failed: see ${link}.`)`. Neither template includes the run's reason.
verification.trigger: A run fails with error "tests failed", or reaches needs_human with a public reason. Watchers receive only the status and UI link, omitting the explicitly required reason.

duplicates.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
duplicates.detail: Both rows require a “comment with the reason,” but the generated messages contain only a generic status and UI link. The run's error or other reason is never included, even when it passes publication checks.
duplicates.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after redaction and private-string checking, with the requested fixed fallback when it cannot be published.
duplicates.failure_scenario: A run fails with a specific gate error; the issue only receives “failed: see [UI link]” and does not explain the failure.

findings.title: Tests require the requested reason to be omitted
findings.detail: The restart test explicitly asserts that the original reason is absent, and the privacy test expects fixed text even when a reason could be redacted. These assertions encode the implementation defect instead of verifying that safe reasons are posted and unsafe reasons are sanitized or replaced.
findings.suggestion: Assert that a safe original reason survives a restart, and separately exercise a credential and a private string in the reason.
findings.failure_scenario: Removing reason handling entirely still passes the tests, while implementing the requested safe reason would fail the current assertion.

verification.evidence: test/issue-queue.test.ts:1370 supplies `error: "original reason"`, but :1392 asserts `expect(h.comments.get(7)?.[1]).not.toContain("original reason")`. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82–83 constructs only `needs you: see ${link}.` or `failed: see ${link}.`, without reading the reason.
verification.trigger: A run reaches needs_human or failed with a safe reason. Omitting that reason passes the test; including the requested safe original reason fails its assertion.

findings.title: Transitions between polls are never recorded
findings.detail: Events are created only from the run's current snapshot during reconciliation. A needs-human or failed state that is resolved before the next poll leaves no durable event to deliver, contrary to the requirement that each transition be a recorded side effect.
findings.suggestion: Record lifecycle transitions durably when they occur, then have polling deliver those records. Add a test that transitions through needs-human or failed and resolves before reconciliation runs.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters needs_human and an owner resolves it before the next queue poll; no needs-you label or comment is ever recorded or posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:25-26 selects needs-you only when `run.status === "needs_human"`; :82 creates its comment under the same current-status condition; :105 reads `store.issueLifecycleRuns()`. No transition history is replayed.
verification.trigger: A run enters needs_human and is resolved between queue polls. Reconciliation sees resolved and never records or posts the needs-you update. This duplicates C9.

findings.title: Blocked publication permanently drops the comment
findings.detail: When the private-strings check rejects a generated body, the effect is marked done without posting the required fixed fallback. The test named "private lifecycle bodies are suppressed durably" explicitly expects this behavior.
findings.suggestion: Create and check a fixed fallback body and keep its delivery pending until it is posted; test that the fallback is posted once.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured private string appears in the generated UI link or run identifier; the issue receives no lifecycle comment and no later poll retries it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:98–100 catches publication rejection with `save(effect, "done")`; line 87 skips recorded effects with `if (effects.has(effect)) continue`. src/gates/publication.ts:77 throws when a private string matches: `if (hit) throw new PrivateError(...)`.
verification.trigger: A configured private string remains in the UI URL or run identifier after sanitization. Publication checking rejects the comment, which is durably marked done without posting the required fixed fallback; later polls and restarts skip it.

findings.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason
findings.detail: Both terminal comments contain only a status and UI link. The request requires a comment with the reason, and the tests explicitly assert that the original reason is absent. Readers cannot tell from the issue why the run failed or what needs attention.
findings.suggestion: Include the recorded reason after credential redaction and the private-strings check, using a fixed fallback when it cannot be published.
findings.failure_scenario: A run reaches needs_human with an actionable question or fails with an error; the issue receives only “needs you: see …” or “failed: see …”.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:82–83 constructs only `events.set("needs_human", `needs you: see ${link}.`)` and `events.set("failed", `failed: see ${link}.`)`. test/issue-queue.test.ts:1392 explicitly asserts the comment does `not.toContain("original reason")`.
verification.trigger: A run fails or reaches needs_human with a safe, actionable reason. Its lifecycle comment always contains only the status and UI link, omitting the explicitly required reason even when publication checks would allow it.

findings.title: Blocked publication text permanently suppresses the comment
findings.detail: When the private-strings check rejects a comment, the effect is marked done without posting the required fixed message. The same happens when a pending body fails its check before delivery. This permanently loses the lifecycle notification rather than providing the safe fallback required by the request.
findings.suggestion: Prepare and publish a fixed, checked fallback message when the original text is blocked, and retain the effect as pending until delivery succeeds.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured UI URL or run ID contains a private string. The label is updated, but no lifecycle comment is ever posted, including after subsequent polls or restarts.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:93–99 checks the generated comment and handles rejection with `save(effect, "done")`; line 87 then skips existing effects. test/issue-queue.test.ts:1562–1570 configures the run ID as private and asserts no comment POST, a `done` checkpoint, and an applied in-progress label.
verification.trigger: The configured UI URL or run ID contains a private string. Labels are reconciled, but the comment is permanently suppressed instead of being replaced with a fixed public message, including after subsequent polls or restarts.

findings.title: Lifecycle writes are restricted to repositories enabled for the issue queue
findings.detail: Reconciliation accepts only repositories listed in githubQueue with trusted accounts, and the only caller is the queue poller, which does not start without that configuration. Runs started directly, through MCP, or through GitHub triggers for other repositories therefore receive no lifecycle labels or durable comments, although the request covers any start path.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and cover linked issues for all supported start paths.
findings.failure_scenario: A configured repository has no issue queue enabled and an owner starts `limitless run` with `Closes #123`; issue 123 never receives the in-progress label or lifecycle comments.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:11–13 defines management as `!!cfg.githubQueue?.trusted.length && cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`. Lines 110 and 116 restrict observation and delivery using `lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo)`. src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:156 also returns immediately when queue repositories or trusted accounts are absent.
verification.trigger: An owner starts a run with `Closes #123` in a configured repository outside githubQueue.repos. Lifecycle reconciliation excludes that issue, so it receives no in-progress label or start comment despite the requirement covering every start path.

findings.title: Lifecycle updates are restricted to configured queue repositories
findings.detail: The request requires updates for “any start path,” but lifecycleManaged requires the repository to be in githubQueue.repos with trusted accounts configured. The reconciler itself is started only when the issue queue is enabled. CLI, MCP, and trigger runs against other repositories therefore receive no lifecycle labels or durable comments.
findings.suggestion: Run lifecycle reconciliation independently of queue admission configuration and include every linked issue from the supported start paths.
findings.failure_scenario: A user starts a CLI run with Closes #42 in a repository not listed in githubQueue.repos; no in-progress label or start comment is posted.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:12–13 requires the repository to match `cfg.githubQueue.repos.some(...)`; line 116 applies `.filter(({ repo }) => lifecycleManaged(cfg, repo))` before creating delivery tasks.
verification.trigger: A CLI run contains `Closes #42` for a repository not listed in githubQueue.repos. The issue is filtered out of lifecycle delivery and receives neither the required in-progress label nor start comment.

findings.title: Blocked publication text silently discards the comment
findings.detail: The request says “If the check blocks the text, post a fixed message without it.” Instead, a publication check failure marks the effect done without posting anything. The same behavior occurs when a pending body fails its later check.
findings.suggestion: Checkpoint and deliver a fixed, safe fallback comment when the original body is blocked.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured UI URL or another generated comment field contains a private string; the check rejects the body and the lifecycle comment is permanently skipped.

verification.evidence: src/gates/publication.ts:76-77 throws on a private-string match: `if (hit) throw new PrivateError(...)`. src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:98-100 catches that rejection with `save(effect, "done"); logFailure(...)`; line 87 prevents reconsideration: `if (effects.has(effect)) continue;`. test/issue-queue.test.ts:1566-1567 explicitly expects no comment POST and a `"done"` checkpoint.
verification.trigger: In a non-discreet repository, cfg.uiUrl or another generated comment field contains a configured private string. Publication validation rejects the body and permanently marks the comment done without posting the required fixed fallback message. The rejection is logged, but the issue receives no comment.

findings.title: A failed run can be re-picked before its failure label is applied
findings.detail: When the latest run failed but the failed label is absent, admission falls back to accepting a trusted priority event after the run's finish time. If the failure-label write is delayed or fails, this permits re-pick before the required failure label and subsequent approval exist.
findings.suggestion: For a failed latest run, require evidence that its failure label was applied and that a trusted priority application followed that label.
findings.failure_scenario: A run fails, its GitHub label write fails, and a trusted user reapplies a priority label before the next poll. The next admission check can start another run without any priority application after the failure label.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:88 defines `failed` from current issue labels. At src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:117–124, an absent failed label selects the fallback requiring only a trusted priority timestamp after finishedAt. Failed label writes merely log and continue at src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:227–234, allowing subsequent queue selection.
verification.trigger: After a run fails, removal of in-progress succeeds but adding limitless:failed fails. A trusted user reapplies priority after finishedAt, and the next poll's failure-label retry also fails. Admission starts another run without any priority application after the failure label.

candidates.title: Failure and needs-human comments omit the reason

candidates.title: Blocked publication text permanently suppresses the comment

candidates.title: Blocked publication text silently discards the comment

candidates.title: A failed run can be re-picked before its failure label is applied

findings.title: An in-flight old worker can still push an ungranted workflow
findings.detail: The new publication guard runs in the worker process. Release matching prevents an old worker from leasing a new job, but it does not cancel a job already leased when the coordinator is upgraded. The old worker can finish that job and push its commit using the previous publication code, before the new coordinator can inspect it. Observing a new release schedules a worker update without aborting the active job.
findings.suggestion: Fence or cancel publication-capable jobs from the previous release during upgrade, and ensure the old worker cannot push after the new policy takes effect.
findings.failure_scenario: A worker leases an edit job on the previous release, the daemon is upgraded while the job is running, and the edit adds .github/workflows/ci.yml without an allowance. The old worker pushes the commit before the upgraded coordinator audits it.

verification.evidence: src/workers/client.ts:963–975 waits for active jobs before updating: `if (updateBlocked()) { await Promise.all(allJobs().map(([, job]) => job.task)); ... await updateWorker(...) }` (the base release has the same behavior at lines 961–973). src/db/workers.ts:314–320 renews held leases without checking release equality: `if (j?.state !== "leased" || j.worker !== w.name) cancelled.push(id); else ... UPDATE ... lease_expires_at=?`. The new guard is worker-local at src/workers/publication.ts:102: `await assertWorkflowPublication(...)`; the base version lacks it and directly executes `"git", "push"` at src/workers/publication.ts:136–144. Publication precedes coordinator reporting: src/workers/client.ts:911 calls `publishAgentChanges`, then lines 928–931 send `${path}/result`.
verification.trigger: An old worker holds an edit lease across a coordinator upgrade and adds an ungranted workflow. Its lease remains renewable and its update waits for the job to finish. The old publication code pushes the workflow before reporting the result, so the upgraded coordinator's subsequent audit cannot prevent that push.

findings.title: Assert that granted workflow changes remain warnings
findings.detail: The allowance test checks only that there is no blocking finding. It would also pass if granting `workflows` accidentally suppressed the `ci-config` finding entirely, so it does not protect the intended advisory audit record.
findings.suggestion: Assert that each granted workflow change produces a `ci-config` finding for the affected path with severity `warn`.
findings.failure_scenario: An allowed workflow edit is delivered without any audit finding because the allowed branch stops emitting `ci-config`; the current test still passes.

verification.evidence: test/gates.test.ts:1826–1828 asserts only `auditDiff(diff("", [file]), { ...ctx, allow: ["workflows"] }).some((f) => f.severity === "block")` is false. An empty findings array also passes. src/gates/audit.ts:354–358 currently emits `rule: "ci-config", severity: ctx.allow?.includes("workflows") ? "warn" : "block"`, but the test does not protect the granted warning.
verification.trigger: A regression suppresses ci-config findings when workflows is allowed; the granted-case assertion still passes despite the missing warning.

candidates.title: Workflow refusal exposes private strings in filenames
candidates.detail: The publication guard includes the raw workflow path in its error before the worker checks private strings. That error is sent as the worker failure reason and can also be logged by the pipeline. A filename containing a configured private string therefore leaves the private-string boundary, even though auditDiff separately detects the private filename.
candidates.suggestion: Redact private strings from the filename before constructing the error, or use the private-string finding to return a sanitized refusal.
candidates.failure_scenario: An agent creates .github/workflows/<private-string>.yml without a workflows allowance. The guard blocks the push but includes the private string in the reported failure reason.

verdicts.evidence: src/git/repos.ts:1534–1538 obtains the finding from `auditDiff(...)` before interpolating it into the error. That function loads private strings at src/gates/audit.ts:207 (`const entries = loadPrivateStrings(ctx.configDir)`) and sanitizes every returned finding: src/gates/audit.ts:446 uses `file: privateMatches(file, protectedText).length ? "[redacted filename]" : file`; line 449 similarly replaces matching details with `"[redacted diagnostic]"`.
verdicts.trigger: A workflow filename containing a configured private string produces a refusal with `[redacted filename]`, preventing the claimed disclosure.

findings.title: Terminal status prevents the scheduler from resuming rollback
findings.detail: The rejection is saved with status needs_human before rollback begins. On daemon restart, Scheduler.start() requeues only running and waiting_input runs, so it never calls executeRun for this checkpoint. A restart after this write can leave the checkout at the rejected merge, or leave the rollback state and draft reporting unfinished. The new tests bypass the scheduler by calling executeRun directly, so they do not exercise the actual restart path.
findings.suggestion: Persist the rejection while the run remains resumable, then mark it needs_human after rollback completes, or explicitly teach scheduler recovery to resume terminal runs with an unfinished rejection checkpoint. Test through a restarted scheduler.
findings.failure_scenario: The daemon exits after the rejection updateRun commits but before reset --hard completes. On startup the run remains needs_human, the scheduler does not requeue it, and the checkout remains at the rejected merged SHA.

verification.evidence: src/pipeline/engine.ts:3505 persists `{ status: "needs_human", ... }` before line 3508 calls `rollbackRejectedMerge(ctx)`. src/scheduler.ts:43 recovers only `status: ["running", "waiting_input"]`; src/db/store.ts:2099 selects work with `WHERE runs.status = 'queued'`.
verification.trigger: Daemon exits after the rejection checkpoint but before reset completes. Startup skips the terminal run, leaving the checkout at the rejected merge instead of finishing rollback.

findings.title: Rollback errors are treated as completed terminal runs
findings.detail: Any ordinary error or abort during rollback returns needs_human without arranging another attempt or recording that cleanup failed in the run error. Because the rejection was already marked terminal, the scheduler will not retry it. A transient Git failure therefore leaves the checkout or persisted head inconsistent indefinitely, while the visible error reports only the original gate regression.
findings.suggestion: Keep an incomplete rollback eligible for recovery and record the rollback failure; transition to the terminal state only after cleanup succeeds.
findings.failure_scenario: git reset or git clean fails after the rejection is persisted, or shutdown aborts either command. executeScopedRun returns needs_human and no scheduler retry finishes the rollback.
