With no bot login, the factory-author exclusion cannot match, so a trusted factory bot's slash command can create and record a run. This also consumes a command after an API error, contrary to the requested retry behavior.
findings.suggestion: Leave comments retryable when the factory identity cannot be established, and process them after a successful identity lookup.
findings.failure_scenario: The configured trusted logins include the factory bot, its comment begins `/limitless `, and the identity lookup fails during polling. The comment creates a run instead of being skipped.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:278 converts identity failure to null with `.catch(() => null)`. Line 280 consequently sets `bot` to null; the exclusion at line 298, `author.toLowerCase() === bot`, cannot match a bot login. Lines 284–285 still parse slash commands, and line 318 calls `factory.createRun`.
verification.trigger: After the query succeeds, identity lookup fails. A trusted factory bot's unedited, post-boundary slash command without a marker passes the author checks and creates a run, assuming no existing claim.

findings.title: Identity failure test misses factory-authored slash commands
findings.detail: The identity failure test explicitly expects a human slash command to run but does not include a trusted factory-authored slash command. Consequently it passes while the factory-author exclusion fails when identity resolution fails.
findings.suggestion: Add a trusted factory-authored slash command during an identity failure and assert that it creates no run or processed record, including after identity recovery.
findings.failure_scenario: The bot is trusted and identity resolution fails; the test suite does not detect that the bot's command is processed.

verification.evidence: test/issue-queue.test.ts:3186–3196 uses `harness()` and owner-authored `commandComment()` while identity throws. The factory-author test instead supplies successful identity resolution (2967–2973). src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:278–280 converts identity failure to `bot = null`; its exclusion is only `author.toLowerCase() === bot` (298), so a trusted bot's slash command passes.
verification.trigger: Identity resolution fails while an unedited, marker-free slash command from a trusted factory bot is newer than the boundary. It can start a run; neither test exercises this combination.

findings.title: Request framing test derives its expected value from the implementation
findings.detail: The polling test constructs its expected request with the same `commentRunRequest` function used by the implementation. The non-queue webhook test does the same, so a regression in the shared builder's prompt framing or source fields can satisfy both comparisons.
findings.suggestion: Assert an independently specified expected request, including the quoted prompt framing, issue source reference, and owner-only allowance.
findings.failure_scenario: The shared builder drops the quoted issue body or changes the prompt framing; both tests compute the same incorrect expected request and pass.

verification.evidence: test/issue-queue.test.ts:2828 computes `const expected = commentRunRequest(...)`, then compares requests against it at 2839. The webhook test also derives its expectation through `commentRunRequest` (3157–3168). Production uses that same builder (src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:306 and src/integrations/github.ts:160).
verification.trigger: The shared builder drops issue context or changes framing: these two comparisons still pass because their expected values change identically. Independent coverage exists elsewhere—test/triage-decisions.test.ts:137–140 explicitly checks the comment's issue body—so this confirms weakness in the cited tests, not absence of all regression coverage.

findings.title: Do not process commands when the factory identity cannot be established
findings.detail: An identity lookup failure is converted to null, after which slash commands still run and the factory-bot author check compares against null. This fails open on a check needed to exclude the factory's own comments.
findings.suggestion: Treat an identity lookup failure as a retryable poll failure and process no comments until the identity is known.
findings.failure_scenario: For an App-backed repository whose bot login is in the trusted list, an identity lookup fails after the issue query succeeds. A bot-authored `/limitless ...` comment without the marker is accepted as a trusted command and creates a run.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:278 uses `.catch(() => null)` and line 280 uses `identity?.kind === "app" ? identity.botLogin.toLowerCase() : null`. The sole bot-author comparison at line 298 therefore fails open, while slash-command parsing at lines 284–285 remains enabled.
verification.trigger: An App bot is trusted and posts an otherwise eligible `/limitless ...` comment without a marker. Identity lookup fails after the query succeeds, so the factory accepts its own command and creates a run.

findings.title: An empty first poll does not establish an enable boundary
findings.detail: When a repository has no open issues, there is no timestamp to store. The first subsequent poll containing an issue becomes the effective initial poll and skips all of its comments, even if they were created after the queue was enabled.
findings.suggestion: Establish a GitHub-time boundary on the first successful empty poll as well, without using the local clock.
findings.failure_scenario: Enable the queue while the repository has no open issues, then create an issue and post a trusted command before the next poll. That poll stores the issue timestamp as the boundary and never starts the command.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:272–275 derives `newest` solely from returned issues and comments and writes the boundary only `if (newest)`. Line 282 processes comments only when the previously read `boundary` exists. test/issue-queue.test.ts:3015–3026 explicitly verifies that an empty poll leaves the boundary null and a command present in the next poll never runs.
verification.trigger: The first successful poll has no open issues. An issue and trusted command arrive before the next poll; that poll establishes the boundary from their timestamps, permanently excluding the command despite its arrival after the first successful poll.

findings.title: Do not reject commands merely containing a factory marker
findings.detail: The substring check rejects any trusted command containing `<!-- limitless-`, even when the comment was authored by a human and the marker is part of the requested work. Such comments are skipped forever.
findings.suggestion: Identify factory-authored comments using their author or a precise factory-comment format instead of searching arbitrary request text.
findings.failure_scenario: A trusted user posts `/limitless investigate <!-- limitless-lifecycle:example -->` after the boundary. The valid command is never processed.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:299 applies `c.body.includes("<!-- limitless-")` independently of authorship; lines 303–304 skip matching comments. It does not distinguish a user's quoted marker from a factory-authored comment.
verification.trigger: An otherwise eligible trusted user posts `/limitless investigate <!-- limitless-lifecycle:example -->` after the boundary. Every poll skips it and no run starts.

findings.title: An empty first poll does not establish the enable boundary
findings.detail: The request says, "on the first successful poll of a repository, store the newest GitHub timestamp in the response" and "Nothing in that first poll runs." When that response contains no open issues, `newest` is absent and no boundary is stored. The first later poll containing an issue is consequently treated as the first poll, so a command posted after queue enablement is skipped permanently as pre-boundary.
findings.suggestion: Establish a GitHub-time boundary on the first successful poll even when there are no open issues, using a GitHub timestamp included in the response.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository has no open issues when the queue first polls. A trusted user then opens an issue and posts `/limitless fix it`; the next poll records that comment's timestamp as the boundary and never runs it.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:272–275 derives `newest` solely from `issues.nodes` and writes the boundary only with `if (newest) factory.store.githubCommentBoundary(repo, newest)`. Line 282 skips comments without an existing boundary; line 301 subsequently skips timestamps `<=` that boundary. test/issue-queue.test.ts:3015 explicitly tests "an empty repository stays uninitialized" and verifies the later command never runs.
verification.trigger: The first successful poll has no open issues. A subsequent issue and command supply the initial boundary, permanently excluding that command despite its creation after polling was enabled.

findings.title: The first poll can still start ordinary issue-queue runs
findings.detail: The request explicitly says "Nothing in that first poll runs." The missing-boundary branch suppresses comment processing, but processing continues into issue eligibility and the candidates loop, which can create a run on that same poll.
findings.suggestion: After successfully establishing a repository's initial boundary, skip run creation for that repository until a subsequent poll.
findings.failure_scenario: On the first successful poll, an open issue has a trusted priority label and otherwise meets queue eligibility. It is added to candidates and started immediately.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:282 guards only comment processing with `boundary`. Ordinary eligibility runs unconditionally at lines 331–336: `if (result.eligible) candidates.push(...)`. Line 398 then executes `await factory.createRun(request, false, undefined, true, admission)` without a first-poll guard.
verification.trigger: An otherwise eligible priority-labelled issue exists on the first successful poll, with capacity available. The queue immediately starts its ordinary issue run, violating the stated requirement that nothing in that first poll runs.

findings.title: A marker in a trusted request suppresses a valid command

findings.suggestion: Identify factory comments by their posting identity or another precise provenance check rather than rejecting arbitrary request text containing the marker prefix.
findings.failure_scenario: A trusted user posts `/limitless fix rendering of <!-- limitless-example -->`; the comment is skipped on every poll and no run is created.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:278–280 uses `.catch(() => null)` and sets `bot` to null on failure. Slash parsing remains enabled at lines 284–285, while the factory-author guard at line 298 compares the author against that null value. src/db/store.ts:1261–1262 persists the resulting run and processed-comment record.

findings.title: Initialize the enable boundary when the first poll has no open issues
findings.detail: An empty successful response leaves the repository without a boundary. The next successful poll is then treated as the initial poll and skips all its comments, including commands created after the repository was enabled. Those commands remain at or before the newly stored boundary and can never run.
findings.suggestion: Establish a durable boundary from GitHub time even when the open-issue result is empty, while preserving the requirement that the initial poll consumes no commands.
findings.failure_scenario: The first successful poll finds no open issues. Before the next poll, a user opens an issue and posts a trusted `/limitless` command. The next poll stores that issue or comment timestamp as the boundary and skips the command permanently.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:272–275 computes the initial timestamp from open issues and comments, then writes it only `if (newest)`. Line 282 skips command processing while the prior boundary is absent; line 301 excludes comments at or before the eventual boundary.
verification.trigger: The initial successful poll has no open issues and stores no boundary. A trusted command posted before the next poll becomes part of the delayed boundary initialization and never runs.

findings.title: An initially empty repository loses its first later command
findings.detail: A successful poll with no open issues leaves the boundary unset. When an issue and command later appear, that poll establishes the boundary using the command timestamp and skips the command permanently. The test at test/issue-queue.test.ts:3015 asserts this behavior instead of checking that a command created after enablement runs.
findings.suggestion: Establish a GitHub-time boundary on the first successful poll even when there are no open issues, and test an issue and command created after that poll.
findings.failure_scenario: The queue is enabled for an empty repository; after its first successful poll, a trusted user opens an issue and posts a command before the next poll. No run is created.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:272–275 computes `newest` from `issues.nodes` and persists it only with `if (newest) factory.store.githubCommentBoundary(repo, newest);`. Line 282 processes comments only when `boundary` exists; line 301 rejects `Date.parse(c.createdAt) <= Date.parse(boundary ?? "")`. test/issue-queue.test.ts:3015 explicitly tests that an empty repository stays uninitialized and its first later command never runs.
verification.trigger: A successful initial poll returns no open issues, leaving no boundary. The next poll sees the newly opened issue and command, establishes a boundary at or after that command, and permanently skips it.

findings.title: Identity lookup failure can allow the factory's own command
findings.detail: An identity failure is converted to null, so the factory-author check cannot exclude its bot login. If that login is also trusted, a slash command authored by the factory can start a run. The identity-failure test covers a human slash command but never tests a trusted bot author.
findings.suggestion: Keep comments retryable when the factory identity cannot be established, or otherwise reliably exclude the factory author; add a test with the bot in the trusted list and identity resolution failing.
findings.failure_scenario: The App identity lookup fails temporarily, the configured trusted list includes the App bot, and an unedited bot-authored `/limitless` comment is returned after the boundary.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:278 converts identity errors with `.catch(() => null)`; line 280 sets `bot` to null without an App identity. Lines 284–285 still parse `/limitless ` commands, while line 298 excludes the factory only through `author.toLowerCase() === bot`. Lines 300–325 allow a trusted author through to `factory.createRun(...)`.
verification.trigger: With an established boundary, identity resolution fails and an otherwise eligible, marker-free App-authored slash command comes from a login in the trusted list. The null bot identity defeats the factory-author exclusion and a run is created.

findings.title: Marker substring rejects legitimate trusted commands
findings.detail: Any command containing `<!-- limitless-` is skipped even when a trusted human authored it. The request only excludes comments posted by the factory; it does not exclude human requests containing marker text. The marker case at test/issue-queue.test.ts:2975 asserts this incorrect exclusion.
findings.suggestion: Identify factory comments by their author rather than rejecting arbitrary request text, and test a human command containing a marker.
findings.failure_scenario: A trusted user posts `/limitless explain <!-- limitless-status -->`; the command remains unprocessed on every poll.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:299 checks `c.body.includes("<!-- limitless-")`, and line 304 executes `continue` for that condition. This check applies to the entire trusted user's command, independently of author identity.
verification.trigger: A trusted user posts an otherwise eligible `/limitless explain <!-- limitless-status -->` command. Its request contains the marker substring, so every poll skips it without creating a run or recording an outcome.

findings.title: Shared-builder expectation cannot detect request framing regressions
findings.detail: The poll test computes its expected request by calling the same builder used by the implementation. A regression in that builder's title, prompt framing, or source reference can therefore affect both actual and expected values and still pass. The non-queue webhook test also compares against that builder.
findings.suggestion: Assert an independently specified request, including its prompt framing, title, source reference and allowed categories, and compare both entry paths with it.
findings.failure_scenario: The builder drops the quoted issue body or changes the comment prompt preface; both sides of the test change together and the test remains green.

verification.evidence: test/issue-queue.test.ts:2828 constructs `const expected = commentRunRequest(...)`; line 2839 asserts `expect(h.requests).toEqual([{ ...expected, sourceRef: { ...expected.sourceRef, via: "queue" } }])`. Production also calls `commentRunRequest` (src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:306). The framing being tested is generated inside that shared function: `prompt: `${GITHUB_PREFACES.comment}\n\n${quoted({ request, issueTitle, issueBody })}`` (src/integrations/github.ts:101).
verification.trigger: If the shared builder drops issueBody or changes the prompt preface, both the actual request and this test's expected request change together, so this assertion remains green.

findings.title: Fail closed when the posting identity cannot be resolved
findings.detail: An identity error is converted to null, after which slash commands are still processed without being able to exclude the factory's App login. The command can create a run or permanently record a refusal, so a later successful identity lookup cannot correct the decision.
findings.suggestion: Leave comments unprocessed when the posting identity cannot be established, and retry on a later poll.
findings.failure_scenario: The App login is in the trusted list, its comment starts with /limitless, and identity resolution fails after the issue query succeeds. The bot-authored command is accepted even though factory-authored comments must never run.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:278 uses `.catch(() => null)` for identity resolution, and line 280 consequently makes `bot` null. The factory-author guard at line 298 is only `author.toLowerCase() === bot`; slash command parsing at lines 284–285 does not require identity resolution.
verification.trigger: After the boundary exists, a trusted App bot authors an unedited, marker-free `/limitless` command and identity lookup fails. The command passes the factory-author guard and reaches run creation. This is the same defect as C7.

findings.title: Establish a boundary when the first poll has no open issues
findings.detail: An empty successful response provides no timestamp, so no boundary is stored. The next poll containing an issue is treated as the first poll and silently skips all its comments, including commands posted after queue enablement.
findings.suggestion: Obtain and persist a GitHub-time boundary even when the open-issue response is empty.
findings.failure_scenario: The queue is enabled while the repository has no open issues. A user then opens an issue and posts a command before the next poll; that poll stores the issue timestamp as the boundary and never runs the command.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:271–275 stores a missing boundary only when timestamps from open issues produce `newest`. Line 282 skips all comments while the previously read `boundary` is absent; line 301 subsequently excludes comments at or before the stored boundary.
verification.trigger: The first successful poll has no open issues and stores nothing. A command posted before the next poll becomes part of that poll's initial boundary and never runs, despite being posted after the first successful poll. This is the same defect as C6.

findings.title: Do not use only open-issue timestamps as the enable boundary
findings.detail: The newest timestamp among currently open issues can be older than the first successful poll. A pre-existing command on a closed issue can therefore have a timestamp after the stored boundary and be treated as new when the issue is reopened.
findings.suggestion: Capture a GitHub-time enable boundary that represents the first successful poll, including when the newest open-issue activity is old.
findings.failure_scenario: The only open issue was last updated Monday. A trusted user comments on a closed issue Tuesday, the queue is enabled Wednesday, and that issue is reopened Thursday. The Tuesday command passes the Monday boundary and starts a run despite predating enablement.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:236 queries only `states:OPEN`. Lines 272–275 derive the permanent boundary from those issues: `.flatMap((i) => [i.updatedAt, ...i.comments.nodes.map((c) => c.createdAt)])`. Line 301 excludes only `Date.parse(c.createdAt) <= Date.parse(boundary ?? "")`.
verification.trigger: An initial poll stores Monday's newest open-issue timestamp. A Tuesday command on a closed issue becomes visible after Thursday's reopening and passes that boundary, although it predates Wednesday's enablement. The requested timestamp mechanism itself permits this case.

findings.title: An initially empty repository loses its first later command
findings.detail: The request says the enable boundary is established on the first successful poll. When that poll has no open issues, no boundary is stored. The first later poll containing an issue instead establishes its boundary and skips all its comments, including commands created after enablement. The added test explicitly expects this loss.
findings.suggestion: Establish a durable GitHub-time boundary even when the initial open-issue response is empty, so later commands can be evaluated against the original enablement.
findings.failure_scenario: The queue successfully polls a repository with no open issues. A user then opens an issue and posts `/limitless build` before the next poll; that poll records the comment timestamp as the boundary and the command never runs.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:275 persists a boundary only `if (newest)`, while line 282 processes comments only when `boundary` exists. test/issue-queue.test.ts:3015–3026 explicitly verifies that an empty poll leaves the boundary null, a later command becomes the boundary, and subsequent polls produce no runs.
verification.trigger: The first successful poll has no open issues. An issue and command appear before the next poll; that command becomes the boundary and is permanently skipped.

findings.title: Identity lookup failure permits commands from the factory bot
findings.detail: The request requires that a command run only if the factory did not post it. An identity error is converted to null, but slash commands are still processed; the factory-author comparison then cannot identify the bot. If the bot login is trusted, its own slash command is recorded and starts a run.
findings.suggestion: Leave commands retryable when the posting identity needed to exclude the factory cannot be confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: An App bot is included in the trusted logins and has posted `/limitless build`; its identity lookup fails during a later poll, so `bot` is null and the comment starts a run.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:278 converts identity failure to null with `.catch(() => null)`; line 280 then sets `bot` to null. The factory-author exclusion at line 298 is only `author.toLowerCase() === bot`, while lines 284–285 still parse slash commands.
verification.trigger: With an established boundary, a trusted factory bot posts an otherwise eligible slash command and identity lookup fails. The bot exclusion fails open and run creation proceeds. Production requires a lookup failure after the authenticated query succeeds, such as a token refresh becoming necessary between calls.

findings.title: A marker anywhere in a valid request silently suppresses it
findings.detail: The command definition accepts any nonempty trusted, unedited request after the boundary. This additional substring check skips even a human-authored command that merely discusses or quotes a Limitless marker, and leaves it unrecorded on every poll.
findings.suggestion: Identify factory comments by their verified author instead of rejecting arbitrary request text containing the marker.
findings.failure_scenario: A trusted user posts `/limitless investigate <!-- limitless-lifecycle:... --> rendering`; it meets the stated command criteria but never starts a run.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:299 unconditionally rejects `c.body.includes("<!-- limitless-")`; lines 294–304 apply this to every parsed command regardless of author or marker placement.
verification.trigger: A trusted user includes `<!-- limitless-lifecycle:... -->` anywhere in an otherwise valid request. Every poll silently skips the command.

findings.title: Polling adds API calls despite the specified single-query mechanism
findings.detail: The request specifies reading comments in the existing query with 'no extra API calls'. Pagination now issues additional GraphQL calls for repositories with more than 100 open issues, and the new identity lookup can also make App authentication requests. This changes the stated API-call and rate-limit characteristics.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile the all-open-issues requirement with the no-extra-calls constraint and implement the agreed behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: A repository has 101 open issues: each poll requests at least two issue pages instead of the existing single issue query.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-queue.ts:233–253 wraps `await query(...)` in a pagination loop: `after = page.pageInfo.hasNextPage ? page.pageInfo.endCursor : null` and `while (after)`. Each query invokes `gh` at lines 176–185.
verification.trigger: A repository with 101 open issues and sufficient API budget makes two issue-list API calls per poll, exceeding the requested existing single-query mechanism.

findings.title: Preserve timeout rerun history when a durable result is replayed
findings.detail: A replayed observation retains its original stage ID, so completion in the resumed stage treats it as an earlier-stage execution. findings.title: Record a rejected timeout rerun as retry_rejected
findings.detail: A timeout rerun whose passing result fails provenance validation carries the rejected attempt in result.retryAttempt, but has no retryOriginal. The history function therefore falls through to rerun_failed, losing the reason the passing attempt was rejected. A targeted probe returned rerun_failed for this state: `bun -e 'import { observationHistory } from "./src/gates/failure-class.ts"; const first={name:"test",command:"bun test",ok:false,timedOut:true,exitCode:null,durationMs:1,output:"timeout"}; const rejected={...first,firstAttempt:first,retryAttempt:{...first,ok:true,timedOut:false}}; console.log(observationHistory({name:"test",verdict:"regressed",blocking:true,result:rejected,firstAttempt:first}));'`.
findings.suggestion: Detect a rejected passing retryAttempt before deriving the timeout rerun history, including when retryOriginal is absent.
findings.failure_scenario: An initial check times out, then its stage rerun passes after changing tracked files or without valid SHA provenance. The observation is finalized with rerun_failed instead of retry_rejected.

verification.evidence: src/gates/run.ts:359–362 preserves a rejected passing attempt as `{ ...original, firstAttempt: original, retryAttempt: result }`. The timeout path calls validateRetry at src/pipeline/engine.ts:1666. src/gates/failure-class.ts:32–35 checks `retryAttempt?.ok` only inside `if (c.retryOriginal)`; otherwise timeout evidence returns `passed ? "rerun_passed" : "rerun_failed"`. compareGates at src/gates/run.ts:532–543 supplies no retryOriginal or retryProvenanceRejected for this path.
verification.trigger: A timeout rerun passes but fails SHA or tracked-cleanliness validation. validateRetry restores the original timed-out failure and retains the passing retryAttempt. Without retryOriginal, observationHistory records rerun_failed instead of retry_rejected.

findings.title: Replay completed in-place results even when the executor cannot resume live work
findings.detail: The request requires that “a kept LAN or in-place handle ... is re-attached on resume” and its stored result recorded before re-execution. The real LAN executor rejects even a completed job when its recorded release SHA, environment, or daemon port differs from the current daemon, so a deploy or configuration change between completion and restart discards the stored result and starts another execution without recording the first failure.

Verifier: 12 candidates, 12 checked, 1 refuted.

findings.title: Inspection failure bypasses executor replacement cleanup
findings.detail: If reconciliation enables the replacement executor and the subsequent launchctl print returns an unknown result, ServiceInspectionError is rethrown before the restoration path runs. The new plist remains installed and enabled, and shutdown is never attempted. The added inspection-reconcile test explicitly expects this state. A failed replacement can therefore leave launchd able to start the replacement on a later login, contrary to the requirement that the restored executor remain unloaded and disabled after a failed install.
findings.suggestion: Attempt the journaled executor shutdown and restoration on this error too. If shutdown cannot be confirmed, retain the journal and report the executor recovery commands without claiming restoration succeeded.
findings.failure_scenario: During service install with an existing executor, launchctl enable succeeds for the replacement, but launchctl print times out. Installation exits with the replacement plist enabled and its journal in phase replacing.

verification.evidence: src/cli/service.ts:375-377 enables the executor before inspection: `await ctl(["enable", ...]); ... if (!(await isLoaded(installed)))`. At :166, unknown inspection throws `ServiceInspectionError`. At :562, `if (error instanceof ServiceInspectionError) throw error;` bypasses `await restore(state)` at :565. The journal was saved as `phase: "replacing"` at :554.
verification.trigger: During executor replacement, enable succeeds and the following print times out. Install exits with the replacement plist enabled and its journal still replacing, bypassing shutdown and restoration.

findings.title: A failed plist inspection is treated as no installed executor
findings.detail: Executor discovery relies on `installedUnits`, which silently skips a plist when `plutil` fails. Deploy then writes no intent and can change the checkout without shutting down the loaded executor. Reconciliation can likewise return successfully without confirming it is off. The existing skip becomes unsafe now that this discovery controls the release boundary.
findings.suggestion: Make executor discovery fail closed when an installed plist cannot be inspected, rather than treating the inspection failure as absence.
findings.failure_scenario: An installed executor's plist cannot be read by `plutil` while its launchd job remains loaded; a deploy skips the intent and proceeds to a different release.

verification.evidence: src/cli/service.ts:208-209 runs plutil with allowFail and uses `if (result.exitCode !== 0) continue;`. At :361-362, executor discovery returns only a recognized unit. Deploy at :873-876 writes intent only inside `if (unit)`, then changes checkout at :894.
verification.trigger: An installed, loaded executor's plist consistently fails plutil inspection. Discovery silently omits it, so deploy changes releases without recording an intent or confirming executor shutdown.

findings.title: A timed-out disable can be accepted as confirmed
findings.detail: `sh` can return both `timedOut: true` and exit code 0, but shutdown checks only the exit code. In that case it treats disable as confirmed and permits rollback to check out older code, even though the disable operation timed out. The same omission affects enable and bootstrap reconciliation.
findings.suggestion: Treat a timeout as failure for every launchctl control operation, including disable, enable, bootout, and bootstrap.
findings.failure_scenario: `launchctl disable` reaches its timeout but exits with code 0 during termination; rollback proceeds and the still-enabled executor can be loaded again at login.

verification.evidence: src/cli/service.ts:339 passes `allowFail: true`; :350-351 accepts disable solely through `if (result.exitCode !== 0) throw ...`. src/util/proc.ts:1205-1206 throws on timeout only when `!opts.allowFail`, and :1220 returns `exitCode` and `timedOut` independently. Rollback awaits shutdown at service.ts:932 before restoring checkout at :949.
verification.trigger: Disable returns exitCode 0 with timedOut true. Shutdown accepts this unconfirmed result and rollback restores the previous checkout, potentially leaving the executor enabled for a later login.

findings.title: Inspection errors bypass executor replacement restoration
findings.detail: After writing the replacement plist and enabling its label, an unknown `launchctl print` result throws `ServiceInspectionError` and bypasses the restoration block. The failed install leaves the replacement enabled, its old plist unrestored, and the journal in `replacing`. If launchd has the replacement loaded or loads it at login, a failed installation leaves an executor running despite the requested disabled restoration guarantee.
findings.suggestion: On inspection failure, attempt the fail-closed executor shutdown and journal restoration; retain the journal and report recovery instructions if shutdown cannot be confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: During executor replacement, `launchctl enable` succeeds but the subsequent `print` times out or returns an unexpected error. The install exits with the replacement enabled instead of restoring the old plist disabled.

verification.evidence: src/cli/service.ts:375-377 performs enable before service inspection. At :166, an unknown inspection throws `ServiceInspectionError`; :562 immediately rethrows that error before the restoration at :565. The replacement plist is already written at :556.
verification.trigger: After replacement enable succeeds, print times out or returns an unexpected error. Install bypasses restoration and leaves the replacement enabled instead of restoring the old plist unloaded and disabled.

findings.title: Source executor arguments are not checked as a complete command
findings.detail: The source-unit test checks only that the plist contains the Bun path and the word executor. It does not check the main.ts path, argument order, or extra arguments, so a source plist that cannot start the executor could pass.
findings.suggestion: Parse the source plist and assert that ProgramArguments equals [bun, app/src/cli/main.ts, "executor"], as the packaged test does for its command.
findings.failure_scenario: installationUnits emits [bun, "executor"] or points at the wrong entry file; the source-unit assertions still pass.

verification.evidence: test/service.test.ts:1085 checks only `expect(content).toContain("<string>executor</string>")`; lines 1086–1090 separately check that the Bun executable appears. No assertion checks the source entry-file argument, argument order, or complete ProgramArguments array. The current implementation supplies the correct command at src/cli/service.ts:304,323: `[join(home, ".bun", "bin", "bun"), join(appDir, "src", "cli", "main.ts"), "serve"]` and `[...args.slice(0, -1), "executor"]`.
verification.trigger: A regression omits or changes the source entry-file argument while retaining the Bun and executor strings and existing environment; these source-unit assertions still pass.

findings.title: Rollback shutdown order is tested only with --now
findings.detail: Every case in the rollback-order test passes now: true. The requested coverage also requires gate and restart failures through the normal draining deploy path, so a regression conditional on that path would not be caught.
findings.suggestion: Run the gate-failure and restart-failure order cases with both now values, asserting executor shutdown precedes checkout restoration and daemon restart.
findings.failure_scenario: A normal deploy restores the previous checkout before disabling the executor, while --now retains the correct order; these tests pass.

verification.evidence: test/deploy.test.ts:1727 always calls `deploy(..., { ...f.opts, executor: true, now: true })` in the rollback-order matrix; line 1741 asserts `expect(f.calls.indexOf(`launchctl disable ${f.service}`)).toBeLessThan(restored)`. The equivalent successful-shutdown ordering assertion is absent for normal deploys. Current production code does share the shutdown-before-restore path (src/cli/service.ts:932,949).
verification.trigger: A regression affecting rollback ordering only without --now could escape the ordering tests. This confirms a coverage gap, not an existing production ordering failure.

findings.title: Interrupted deploy is not followed by service installation in the test
findings.detail: This test verifies that interruption leaves a deploying intent, but stops before invoking service install. The separate install test constructs an intent manually, so it does not verify the complete interrupted-deploy-to-install recovery sequence requested.
findings.suggestion: After the interrupted deploy, invoke service install using the retained intent and assert shutdown occurs before installation and reconciliation occurs after daemon health.
findings.failure_scenario: An intent produced by an interrupted deploy is not consumed correctly by the next service install, despite the independently constructed install fixture passing.

verification.evidence: test/deploy.test.ts:1755 invokes the interrupted deploy, but the test ends at line 1766 after intent and no-rollback assertions without calling install. The separate install test uses `migration("intent-install", "executor")` (test/service.test.ts:1172); its fixture manually writes the intent with `writeFileSync(intentPath, JSON.stringify({...}))` before `service.install(...)` (test/service-migration-support.ts:487-497).
verification.trigger: A mismatch between interrupted deploy's persisted state and installation recovery could escape these independently constructed tests. The requested deploy-interruption-to-install recovery sequence is untested; an actual recovery failure is not established.

findings.title: Do not treat failed plist inspection as proof that no executor exists
findings.detail: Executor discovery relies on installedUnits, which silently skips a plist when plutil fails. Deploy then writes no intent and proceeds with checkout changes; reconciliation likewise treats the executor as absent. A loaded executor can consequently survive a rollback without being disabled, including across the next login.
findings.suggestion: Fail closed when executor discovery cannot inspect a potentially relevant installed plist, before changing the checkout or declaring reconciliation successful.
findings.failure_scenario: The executor is loaded from an installed plist, but plutil times out or fails to read that plist during deployment. Discovery returns no executor, so a failed deploy restores the previous checkout without shutting it down or recording an intent.

verification.evidence: src/cli/service.ts:209 silently skips failed plist inspection: `if (result.exitCode !== 0) continue;`. Deploy records intent only when discovery finds a unit (:873-876). Its rollback rediscovery at :925-927 has the same behavior; shutdown runs only `if (intent)` (:929-932), while previous checkout restoration follows at :948-949.
verification.trigger: Plutil repeatedly fails or times out with a nonzero exit for a loaded executor's plist. A subsequent deploy failure restores the previous checkout without executor shutdown or a durable intent.

findings.title: Restore or disable the executor when inspection fails during replacement
findings.detail: The ServiceInspectionError branch bypasses the replacement cleanup after the new plist has been written and the executor has been enabled. For a fresh installation there is no migration journal to trigger recovery on the next invocation.

findings.title: Inspection failure bypasses executor replacement restoration
findings.detail: The request requires that a failed executor replacement restore the old plist and leave the executor unloaded and disabled. After the replacement plist is written, reconcileExecutor enables its label before inspecting whether it is loaded. If that inspection returns an unknown state, ServiceInspectionError bypasses the restoration block entirely. The install fails with the replacement still enabled and potentially loaded, and its journal remains in the replacing phase.
findings.suggestion: Route executor inspection failures through a fail-closed restoration path that attempts shutdown and retains the journal if shutdown cannot be confirmed.
findings.failure_scenario: During executor replacement, launchctl enable succeeds but launchctl print times out or returns an unrecognized error. Installation exits without disabling the replacement or restoring the old plist.

verification.evidence: src/cli/service.ts:554-557 writes the replacement plist and calls `executor.reconcileExecutor(true)`. That helper enables before inspecting (375-377). findings.title: A failed daemon replacement leaves the existing executor running
findings.detail: The request says that “A failed install never leaves an executor running on an unconfirmed release.” Installation processes and health-checks the daemon before reaching the executor entry. If daemon replacement or its health check fails, the function restores the daemon and throws without shutting down the existing executor. This is especially consequential after a packaged upgrade, when the old executor process and the newly started or restored daemon can refer to different releases.
findings.suggestion: Ensure executor shutdown is attempted and confirmed on failed installation paths before returning, including failures before the executor's own replacement begins.
findings.failure_scenario: An existing executor is loaded, a packaged upgrade changes the executable, and service install fails while waiting for the replacement daemon to become healthy. The command exits while the old executor remains loaded and enabled.

verification.evidence: src/cli/service.ts:305 initializes installation units with the daemon; the executor is appended at 320-324. The loop waits for daemon health at 559 before reaching executor shutdown at 541 in its later iteration. On daemon failure, `restore(state)` at 565 restores only that migration. The outer lifecycle returns at 855 before `previous` is assigned, so its catch exits via `if (!previous) throw error` at 924 without executor shutdown.
verification.trigger: With an existing executor loaded and enabled and no pending recovery journal, a packaged service upgrade fails while waiting for daemon health. Installation restores the daemon unit and exits before processing the executor, leaving it loaded and enabled despite the failed installation.

A failed replacement can therefore leave launchd able to start the replacement on a later login, contrary to the requirement that the restored executor remain unloaded and disabled after a failed install.

candidates.title: A failed plist inspection is treated as no installed executor
candidates.detail: Executor discovery relies on `installedUnits`, which silently skips a plist when `plutil` fails. Deploy then writes no intent and can change the checkout without shutting down the loaded executor. Reconciliation can likewise return successfully without confirming it is off. The existing skip becomes unsafe now that this discovery controls the release boundary.

candidates.failure_scenario: An installed executor's plist cannot be read by `plutil` while its launchd job remains loaded; a deploy skips the intent and proceeds to a different release.

candidates.title: A timed-out disable can be accepted as confirmed

candidates.suggestion: Treat a timeout as failure for every launchctl control operation, including disable, enable, bootout, and bootstrap.
candidates.failure_scenario: `launchctl disable` reaches its timeout but exits with code 0 during termination; rollback proceeds and the still-enabled executor can be loaded again at login.

Verifier: 19 candidates, 19 checked, 1 refuted.

findings.title: Release-intent replay bypasses lease-time validation
findings.detail: Reconciliation delegates a pending release to `reconcileLeaseIntent`, which can replay the release with `client.write` without a GitHub-time sample or `beforeSend` predicate. Both startup recovery and ordinary operations use that path, so an expired generation can mutate the claim after its lease window has closed.
findings.suggestion: Ensure release replay uses the same fresh time decision and send-time revalidation as other same-generation writes.
findings.failure_scenario: A release intent is journaled, the process stops before sending it, and recovery runs more than ten minutes later while the old tip remains current. Recovery writes the expired generation's release without checking whether it is renewable.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:65 calls `recoverLeases({ client, store })`; :89 calls `reconcileLeaseIntent({ client, store, signal }, repo, ref)`. The release replay at src/integrations/lease-store.ts:118–121 invokes `client.write(repo, ref, read.tip, intent.record, { signal, onCommit: ... })` without a time check or `beforeSend` hook.
verification.trigger: A pending release still matches the confirmed GitHub tip after the generation expires. Startup recovery or pre-operation reconciliation replays it without requiring a renewable sample.

findings.title: Renewal loop omits recovered confirmed leases
findings.detail: The loop iterates only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated by writes applied in this manager instance. Confirmed held rows loaded at startup, and acquisitions confirmed by intent reconciliation, never enter that map. Even if `active` would accept their handles, the loop never renews them.
findings.suggestion: Enumerate confirmed held rows when starting or reconciling and make their handles available to the renewal loop.
findings.failure_scenario: A manager restarts with a confirmed held lease and starts the loop. Every tick skips that lease; it expires even though the associated run is active.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:49 initializes `const handles = new Map<string, LeaseHandle>()`. Recovery at :64–70 does not populate it. Registration occurs only on a direct applied write at :192: `handles.set(key(repo, ref), held)`. The renewal loop at :242 iterates only `handles.values()`.
verification.trigger: Restart with a confirmed held lease, then start the loop without another successful acquisition or mutation. No handle is registered, so every tick skips renewal even when the run is active.

findings.title: A different run cannot reconcile an earlier pending acquisition
findings.detail: The cross-run check returns `refused` before reconciliation whenever the existing row has an intent. This violates the requirement to reconcile pending intents before every operation, and prevents the caller from clearing a dropped first acquisition unless a separate loop happens to run.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile the existing intent under the mutex before deciding whether the row blocks the requested run.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A leaves an unconfirmed acquisition intent on an absent ref and ends. Run B calls `acquire` before the renewal loop is started; it receives `refused` indefinitely even though reconciliation would drop A's intent and allow B to acquire generation 1.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:107 returns early: `if (row && row.runId !== want.run && (row.intent || row.confirmed?.state === "held")) return refused;`. Reconciliation occurs afterward at :108. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:113–116 would drop an acquisition intent when the ref remains absent; leases.ts:91 would then forget the unconfirmed row.
verification.trigger: Run A leaves an unresolved acquisition intent on an absent ref. Before loop reconciliation, repeated acquire calls from run B return refused without reconciling or clearing A's intent, blocking B.

findings.title: Reconciled and recovered leases are never registered for renewal
findings.detail: The renewal loop iterates only the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated solely by an immediately applied write. Recovery or later reconciliation can confirm a held acquisition without adding a handle to that map. Confirmed held rows already present when the manager starts are likewise omitted. Those leases therefore receive no periodic renewal even when the active hook would return true.
findings.suggestion: Register confirmed held handles after recovery and successful reconciliation, and ensure the loop can discover existing confirmed held rows.
findings.failure_scenario: An acquisition returns `unconfirmed`, then the next tick reconciles its intent as applied. The row is held, but no handle is in `handles`, so subsequent ticks never renew it and the lease expires.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:186 returns immediately for `result.kind === "unconfirmed"`, before handle registration at :192. The reconciliation wrapper at :87–92 handles loss and dropped intents but never registers confirmed handles. At :240–242 the loop reconciles intents, then renews only `handles.values()`.
verification.trigger: An initial acquisition returns unconfirmed but reached GitHub. A loop tick later confirms it as applied. The held row has no registered handle, so subsequent ticks never renew it.

findings.title: A different run bypasses reconciliation of a pending intent
findings.detail: The cross-run early return occurs before reconciliation. The request requires every operation to reconcile pending intents first and return `wait` while an intent remains unresolved. Here a failed first acquisition by run A can leave an intent that run B never attempts to settle, so B is refused even when reconciliation would drop the intent and permit acquisition.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile the row before applying the cross-run ownership check, then re-read the row and decide whether it can be forgotten or must be refused.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A has a pending acquisition intent on an absent ref and ends. Run B calls acquire before the renewal loop has reconciled it; the manager returns `refused: live` without checking GitHub or dropping A's abandoned intent.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:107 checks a different run's pending intent and executes `return refused` before :108's `await reconcile(repo, ref, signal)`. The refusal is defined at :95 as `{ kind: "refused", reason: "live" }`.
verification.trigger: Run B acquires while run A's pending acquisition remains on an absent ref. It receives refused: live without a GitHub reconciliation read, even when reconciliation could drop the abandoned intent and permit acquisition.

findings.title: A second moved result marks ownership lost without checking for supersession
findings.detail: After two moved outcomes that are not classified as same-holder writes, the code marks any confirmed row lost regardless of the moved tip's generation or identity. The invariant permits loss only when a moved record supersedes confirmed ownership. A malformed tip or an older-generation tip does not establish that the confirmed generation was superseded.
findings.suggestion: Classify the second moved tip against the confirmed generation and identity before marking the row lost; preserve ownership when supersession is not established.
findings.failure_scenario: A confirmed generation 2 write encounters two moved responses whose tips are malformed or generation 1. The manager marks generation 2 lost and calls `onLost` despite having no superseding record.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:203–208 checks same-holder equality, then executes `if (++moved < 2) continue;` followed by `if (row?.confirmed && row.runId === want.run) { lose(row, result.tip); return { kind: "superseded", tip: result.tip }; }`. No superseding-generation check guards this loss.
verification.trigger: Two writes return moved tips containing malformed or older-generation records, while the intervening fresh read permits another write. The second moved result marks confirmed ownership lost and invokes onLost without evidence of supersession.

findings.title: An exception in one renewal tick rejects the timer callback
findings.detail: The async interval callback has no error handling. A thrown clock, store, client, or hook error rejects the callback without an observer and skips the remaining leases for that tick. Depending on runtime unhandled-rejection behavior, this can terminate the process; otherwise other active leases silently miss renewal.
findings.suggestion: Observe and report tick failures and isolate per-ref work so one failed operation does not prevent other leases from being processed.
findings.failure_scenario: One lease's `active` hook or clock sample throws during a tick while another active lease also needs renewal. The callback rejects and the second lease is skipped.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:239–243 installs `timer.set(async () => { ... for (const h of handles.values()) if (current(h) && next.active(h)) await manager.update(h, {}); }, LEASE.renewMs);` without exception handling.
verification.trigger: An active hook or renewal clock sample throws for an earlier lease. The timer callback rejects, skipping subsequent leases for that tick and leaving an unhandled rejection.

findings.title: Release intent replay bypasses send-time lease validation
findings.detail: `reconcileLeaseIntent` can replay a pending release with `client.write` without a `beforeSend` hook. Calling it here permits a release of an expired generation after an outage or restart, without the fresh renewable decision and immediate send-time revalidation required for same-generation writes.
findings.suggestion: Provide reconciliation with a time-validating send hook for release replay, and re-decide when validation fails.
findings.failure_scenario: A release intent is persisted before its write, the process stops for longer than the lease duration, and recovery finds the old tip unchanged. Reconciliation sends the release without checking whether the generation is still renewable.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:65 calls `recoverLeases({ client, store })`; line 89 likewise delegates reconciliation without time validation. src/integrations/lease-store.ts:118–121 replays release using `client.write(..., { signal, onCommit: ... })`, omitting beforeSend. src/integrations/claim-ref.ts:206–208 aborts only when `opts.beforeSend?.()` returns false.
verification.trigger: A persisted release survives a restart longer than the lease duration. If its before-tip remains unchanged, recovery sends and confirms the release despite the generation no longer being renewable.

findings.title: Cross-run requests bypass pending-intent reconciliation
findings.detail: A row belonging to another run is refused before its pending intent is reconciled. An unresolved intent must instead be reconciled first and return wait while pending; if it resolves as a dropped, never-confirmed acquisition, the next run must be able to acquire. The test at test/leases.test.ts:169 explicitly expects the premature refusal and unchanged intent, thereby asserting the defect.
findings.suggestion: Reconcile pending intents before deciding whether another run can acquire, and test both unresolved and dropped intents from the next run.
findings.failure_scenario: Run A has an unconfirmed first-acquisition intent and run B attempts the same ref. B receives refused without a GitHub read, even if reconciliation would drop A's intent and permit B to acquire.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:107 returns refused when `row.runId !== want.run && (row.intent || row.confirmed?.state === "held")`; reconciliation occurs only afterward at line 108: `const settled = await reconcile(repo, ref, signal);`.
verification.trigger: Run A has a pending first-acquisition intent and run B requests the same ref. B is refused before reconciliation can drop A's unchanged intent and forget its never-confirmed row, violating the required reconciliation-first behavior.

findings.title: Renewal loop omits recovered confirmed leases
findings.detail: The loop enumerates only the in-memory handles map, which is populated by successful writes in this manager instance. Confirmed held rows present after startup or created by reconciliation of an unconfirmed acquisition are never added to that map, so the loop never renews them. The tests cover reconciliation of an update after an already successful acquisition, but do not cover a recovered held row or an acquisition first confirmed by reconciliation.
findings.suggestion: Populate or derive loop handles from confirmed held rows, and add tests for startup recovery and an unconfirmed acquisition resolved by a tick.
findings.failure_scenario: An acquisition reaches GitHub but its response is lost; a later tick reconciles the intent to held. Subsequent ticks never renew that lease, so it expires despite the active hook returning true.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:49 initializes `const handles = new Map<string, LeaseHandle>();`. Only the direct applied-write path populates it at :192: `handles.set(key(repo, ref), held);`. Reconciliation at :89 calls `reconcileLeaseIntent({ client, store, signal }, repo, ref)` without registering a handle. The loop at :242 renews only `for (const h of handles.values())`.
verification.trigger: An initial acquisition succeeds remotely but returns unconfirmed. A tick confirms its intent, but never adds its handle to the renewal map. Subsequent ticks skip the lease even when active would return true, allowing it to expire.

findings.title: Replayed releases bypass lease-time revalidation
findings.detail: Reconciliation can replay a pending release through `reconcileLeaseIntent`, whose replay write has no time sample or before-send predicate. Calling it before every operation and on every tick therefore permits a same-generation release after the lease window and renewable period have expired. The release expiry test exercises only a newly initiated release, not a pending release replay.
findings.suggestion: Ensure replayed releases use the same fresh time decision and before-send guard as other same-generation writes, and test expiry before replay and while its commit is in flight.
findings.failure_scenario: A release intent is persisted before its ref update, the process pauses beyond lease expiry, and a later tick reconciles it while the ref still points to the old tip. The replay sends the expired generation's release without checking GitHub time.

verification.evidence: src/integrations/leases.ts:89 delegates to `reconcileLeaseIntent({ client, store, signal }, repo, ref)`. In src/integrations/lease-store.ts:113-121, when the tip matches the release intent's confirmed predecessor, reconciliation calls `client.write(repo, ref, read.tip, intent.record, { signal, onCommit: ... })` without `beforeSend`. src/integrations/claim-ref.ts:206-208 only aborts when `opts.beforeSend?.()` returns false.
verification.trigger: A pending release retains its confirmed predecessor as the remote tip. After a pause beyond expiry, loop reconciliation replays the release without sampling GitHub time or checking the same-generation send predicate.

findings.title: Mutant cases explicitly accept two winners
findings.detail: The concurrent-create and takeover tests change their expected winner count to two when the unconditional-ref-write mutant is enabled. Consequently those mutant cases pass while exhibiting the violation, contrary to the requested mutation check that these tests fail against the mutant.

findings.title: A different run cannot reconcile a pending acquisition

This violates the requirement that only a superseding record establishes loss and clears the confirmed ownership on an uncertain result.
candidates.suggestion: Classify the second moved tip against the confirmed run, member and generation before marking loss; return a non-loss result when it does not establish supersession.
candidates.failure_scenario: A confirmed generation 2 write encounters two concurrent ref movements, and the second returned tip is malformed or generation 1. The manager marks generation 2 lost and calls `onLost` even though the returned tip does not establish a superseding generation.

candidates.title: An exception in the renewal timer becomes an unhandled rejection
candidates.detail: The async interval callback has no rejection handler. A thrown database, clock, client, or hook error rejects the callback, stops processing the remaining leases for that tick, and can terminate the process under an unhandled-rejection policy. There is no reporting or controlled retry of the failure.
candidates.suggestion: Handle and report failures from timer work explicitly, and ensure one failed ref does not silently prevent the other refs from being processed.
candidates.failure_scenario: A clock read throws while renewing the first active lease. The timer callback rejects and later active leases are skipped for that tick; the rejection may terminate the daemon.

candidates.title: A different run is refused before the pending intent is reconciled
candidates.detail: The cross-run guard runs before reconciliation, so a pending intent returns `refused` rather than `wait` and cannot be resolved by that acquisition. The test for a pending old run explicitly expects this behavior, masking the violation of the requirement to reconcile pending intents before every operation.
candidates.suggestion: Reconcile first, return wait while the intent remains pending, and only then evaluate the confirmed row and fresh tip. Test both unresolved and dropped intents when a different run acquires.
candidates.failure_scenario: Run A has an unconfirmed first acquisition whose intent can now be dropped; run B calls acquire before the loop runs and is refused instead of reconciling and acquiring.

candidates.title: The renewal loop omits confirmed leases recovered without an in-memory handle
candidates.detail: The loop iterates only handles created by an applied write in this manager instance. Recovery and intent reconciliation can confirm a held row without adding a handle, so that lease is never passed to `active` or renewed. The recovery tests cover loss and an update on an already registered handle, but do not cover a recovered or reconciled acquisition becoming eligible for renewal.
candidates.suggestion: Populate or derive renewal handles from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation, and test a recovered acquisition through a renewal tick.
candidates.failure_scenario: An acquisition returns unconfirmed, then the loop reconciles its intent as applied; subsequent ticks never renew that confirmed lease because no handle was inserted into `handles`.

candidates.title: Mutation tests expect the broken two-winner result
candidates.detail: The unconditional-ref-write cases explicitly expect two winners and therefore pass when the single-holder invariant is broken. The request requires the concurrent-create and takeover tests to fail against that mutant; these cases instead assert the mutant's defect as success.
candidates.suggestion: Use the same one-winner assertions for the normal implementation and mutation check, and verify that running them with the unconditional-write mutant fails.
candidates.failure_scenario: The fake allows both concurrent writes unconditionally; both acquisitions report held at the same generation, yet the mutant test passes.

candidates.title: Replayed release bypasses the lease-time send check
candidates.detail: The manager delegates pending-intent reconciliation to `reconcileLeaseIntent`, which replays a release using `client.write` without a `beforeSend` hook or a fresh GitHub-time sample. A release interrupted before its ref update can therefore be sent after the confirmed generation has expired. That violates the same-generation send-time check and can publish a released tip after the holder's authority has ended.
candidates.suggestion: Require the same fresh-time decision and immediate pre-send revalidation when replaying a release, and leave the intent pending when that authority cannot be confirmed.
candidates.failure_scenario: A release commit is journaled before its ref update, the process stops for longer than the lease expiry, and reconciliation finds the old held tip unchanged. It replays the release without checking expiry; a different run can then acquire the released tip.

candidates.title: Renewal loop omits recovered confirmed leases
candidates.detail: The loop renews only handles inserted into the in-memory `handles` map by an applied write in this manager instance. Creation and reconciliation do not populate that map for previously confirmed held rows or for an acquisition whose unconfirmed intent is later reconciled as applied. Those leases never receive automatic renewal unless another operation happens to write them first.
candidates.suggestion: Populate or derive loop handles from confirmed held rows, including rows confirmed during recovery and reconciliation.
candidates.failure_scenario: An acquisition updates GitHub but returns `unconfirmed`; the next tick reconciles its intent to applied. Subsequent ticks never renew that confirmed lease because no handle was added to `handles`.

candidates.title: Different-run acquisition skips pending-intent reconciliation
candidates.detail: The early different-run check returns `refused` whenever the row has an intent, before reconciliation runs. An unresolved intent is required to yield `wait`, and a dropped never-confirmed acquisition must be forgotten so another run can acquire. This path does neither; without a running renewal loop, the stale intent can block the next run indefinitely.
candidates.suggestion: Reconcile the row before classifying a different-run acquisition, returning wait while unresolved and applying the normal dropped-intent cleanup.
candidates.failure_scenario: Run A leaves an unconfirmed first-acquisition intent whose GitHub ref is still absent. Run B calls acquire before the loop reconciles it and receives `refused: live` instead of reconciling the dropped intent and acquiring the absent ref.

candidates.title: Reconcile another run’s pending intent before refusing
candidates.detail: The request says, “Before every operation, under the ref mutex, a row's pending intent goes through #952's reconcileLeaseIntent” and unresolved intents return `wait`. This early return instead refuses a different run without attempting reconciliation, even when the pending acquisition can be dropped and its never-confirmed row forgotten.
candidates.suggestion: Reconcile the row before deciding whether its run or confirmed ownership prevents the acquisition.
candidates.failure_scenario: Run A has an unconfirmed first acquisition whose write did not move the ref. Run B acquires the same ref after it becomes readable; it receives `refused: live` rather than reconciling A's dropped intent and proceeding.

candidates.title: Restore confirmed handles for the renewal loop
candidates.detail: The request requires the loop to update “each confirmed `held` handle whose `active` hook is true.” The loop only visits the in-memory `handles` map, which is populated by writes applied in this manager instance. Existing confirmed rows after restart, and acquisitions confirmed by intent reconciliation, never enter that map.
candidates.suggestion: Populate or derive renewal handles from confirmed held rows after recovery and reconciliation.
candidates.failure_scenario: A manager restarts with a confirmed held lease, or an unconfirmed acquisition is confirmed on a later tick. Even with `active` returning true, subsequent ticks never renew that lease and it expires.

candidates.title: Revalidate time before replaying a pending release
candidates.detail: The request requires that “Immediately before the `updateRefs` send” the manager revalidate the applicable time predicate. `reconcileLeaseIntent` can replay a release by calling `client.write` without a `beforeSend` hook or a GitHub-time check; this path is also invoked during initial recovery. A release intent left before its send can consequently be written after the generation has expired.
candidates.suggestion: Ensure release replay obtains and revalidates the same-generation time authorization before sending, including during recovery.
candidates.failure_scenario: A release is journaled, the process stops before updating the ref, and recovery runs more than ten minutes later while the ref is unchanged. Recovery sends the stale same-generation release without checking whether renewal is still permitted.

candidates.title: Do not mark ownership lost for every second moved result
candidates.detail: The request says “Only `moved` to a superseding record means lost.” After two non-matching `moved` outcomes, this branch marks any confirmed row lost without checking whether the second tip supersedes its generation and identity.
candidates.suggestion: Classify the returned tip against confirmed ownership before marking the lease lost; return a non-loss result when it does not supersede it.
candidates.failure_scenario: A confirmed generation encounters two moved results whose final tip is malformed or has a lower generation. The manager marks the confirmed lease lost and calls `onLost` despite having no superseding record.

findings.title: Treat browser availability as a positive setup outcome
findings.detail: The engine labels the browser available whenever a preview exists and no `browser_unavailable` event was recorded. That event only covers failures while constructing the MCP configuration; it does not establish that the MCP server or Chromium subsequently started successfully. A verifier that reports a genuine browser startup failure as blocked will therefore have its result converted to unclear and sent into an implementation feedback round.
findings.suggestion: Persist and use a positive, same-invocation browser setup outcome, and retain environment-block handling when successful setup cannot be established.
findings.failure_scenario: The preview starts and browserMcp produces a configuration, but the MCP server or Chromium fails to launch. No `browser_unavailable` warning is emitted, so a marked browser check reported blocked becomes unclear even though the browser was unavailable.

findings.title: A superseded unsent question set can never be published later
findings.detail: An unsent question effect is permanently marked done when its run temporarily stops waiting. If the run later returns to waiting with the same unanswered question IDs, observe() sees the existing effect and never creates another publication. The same problem occurs after recovery establishes that a stale POST was not accepted. The run can therefore remain waiting indefinitely without its questions appearing on the issue.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish a superseded effect with no confirmed publication from a completed publication, and allow a fresh eligible waiting episode to publish the set after any uncertain prior POST has been recovered.
findings.failure_scenario: A run enters waiting_input with question 42, but its pending comment has not been posted. The run temporarily changes to running, so reconciliation marks the effect done. verification.evidence: src/integrations/issue-lifecycle.ts:355–358: `let stale = pending.state === "recovering" || !eligible(); if (stale && !pending.page) { save(effect, "done"); continue; }`. findings.title: Retired unsent question sets cannot be published if they become eligible again
findings.detail: Superseding an unsent question effect marks it done, and observe() will never create that effect again because it already exists. A temporary linkage or status change can therefore permanently suppress a question set that was never posted.
findings.suggestion: Distinguish superseded unsent effects from completed publications and allow the same set to be scheduled again when it becomes eligible.
findings.failure_scenario: A waiting run has a pending question publication, loses its issue link before the POST, and later regains the same link while the question remains open. The effect is done without a comment, so subsequent polls never publish that question set.

findings.title: Privacy reinspection can close an uncertain POST without recovery

findings.failure_scenario: GitHub accepts a question comment but the response is lost. Before the next poll, private-string configuration becomes unreadable or changes to match the stored body. Reinspection fails, the checkpoint is marked done, and the accepted comment is never recovered.
